meta.blurb: Newland Archer is about to announce his engagement to the perfect bride when her scandalous cousin, Countess Olenska, appears in the opera box. In a society that never says what it means, he begins to want what he must not have.
meta.bible: Newland Archer: a young New York lawyer, from an old family, thoughtful, restless and well-mannered. May Welland: his fiancée and later his wife, pretty, kind, loyal, apparently innocent but wiser than she seems. Ellen Olenska: May's cousin, the Countess Olenska, who has left her husband and returned from Europe; honest, charming and unconventional. Count Olenski: Ellen's Polish husband, who never appears. Mrs Welland: May's mother. Mr Welland: May's father. Mrs Manson Mingott: the huge, fearless grandmother of May and Ellen. Mrs Archer: Newland's mother. Janey: Newland's sister. Julius Beaufort: a rich, charming banker whose bank fails. Regina Beaufort: his wife. Sillerton Jackson: an old man who knows all the gossip. Lawrence Lefferts: a fashionable society man. Mr Letterblair: the old family lawyer who employs Archer. Henry van der Luyden and Louisa van der Luyden: the most respected couple in New York society. Monsieur Rivière: a Frenchman, the Count's secretary, who helped Ellen to escape. Dallas: Archer's eldest son. Fanny Beaufort: Julius Beaufort's daughter, who marries Dallas. Academy of Music: the New York opera house. Faust: the opera. Grace Church: where May and Archer marry. St Augustine: the town in Florida where May spends the winter. Newport: the seaside resort. Boston, Paris, Europe, Florida, New York, Washington. Metropolitan Museum. Invalides: the golden dome in Paris near Ellen's home. Duke of St Austrey: an English guest of the van der Luydens, who admires Ellen at their dinner. Medora Manson: Ellen's aunt. Fifth Avenue: where Mrs Mingott's huge house stands, far uptown. Boston Common: where Archer and Ellen sit on a bench. Newport: the Wellands' summer house by the sea, with an archery party where May wins the prize and a lighthouse that Archer watches Ellen look toward. Hudson: the river Archer crosses by ferry to meet Ellen's train from Washington. Metropolitan Museum: where Archer tells Ellen he loves her, among glass cases of ancient cups. Fixed facts in order: the engagement is announced at the Beauforts' ball; the van der Luydens receive Ellen at a dinner for the Duke; Archer persuades Ellen to give up her divorce; he visits May at St Augustine; he meets Monsieur Rivière and Ellen in Boston; he marries May at Grace Church; Beaufort's bank fails; Mrs Mingott has a stroke; Ellen refuses to be Archer's secret love and goes back to Europe to live in Paris; May is expecting a child and told Ellen two weeks before; May gives a farewell dinner for Ellen; Dallas is born in the spring; Archer and May have two more children; May dies of a fever caught nursing a child; Dallas marries Fanny Beaufort; Archer and Dallas visit Paris; Archer will not go up to Ellen's fifth-floor apartment near the Invalides and walks back alone to his hotel. Lawrence Lefferts. Mrs Lefferts. Voice and tone: elegant, gently ironic and sad; the rules of society are never spoken aloud; the love between Archer and Ellen is never consummated, and there is no violence; the ending is quiet and bitter-sweet.
chapters: A Late Arrival at the Opera

beats.scene: Archer enters a crowded opera house after the curtain has gone up
beats.summary: Newland Archer, a young lawyer, arrives late at the opera on a winter night, as fashion demands.

beats.scene: May Welland in white sits in a box holding lilies of the valley
beats.summary: Archer sees May Welland, the girl he is going to marry, in her family's box, dressed in spotless white.

beats.scene: A slender dark-haired woman in blue velvet sits beside May in the box
beats.summary: Beside May sits a stranger in a plain dark gown: her cousin Ellen, Countess Olenska, just back from Europe.

beats.scene: Lefferts and old Sillerton Jackson whisper together in the club box
beats.summary: In the club box Lefferts and old Sillerton Jackson whisper that the Countess has left her husband.

beats.scene: Archer listens to the singer on the stage, his face thoughtful
beats.summary: Archer sees that the old families prefer silence to truth and fear that Ellen will bring trouble to them all.

beats.scene: Archer rises in the club box and looks across at the Welland box
beats.summary: Archer decides that the best answer to the gossip is to announce his engagement at once, to show that the family stands together.

beats.scene: Archer walks along the curved corridor behind the boxes
beats.summary: Walking round the theatre, Archer thinks of the months he has waited to speak of his engagement openly.

beats.scene: Archer bows to Mrs Welland and the ladies inside the family box
beats.summary: Archer slips into the box, where May's mother greets him and May's face lights with joy.

beats.scene: Ellen holds out her hand to Archer in the shadow of the box
beats.summary: Ellen greets Archer simply and reminds him that they knew each other as children.

beats.scene: May blushes and nods as Archer speaks quietly to her
beats.summary: Archer asks May to let him announce the engagement at the Beauforts' ball that night, and she agrees.

beats.scene: The Beauforts' great ballroom blazes with candles, flowers and jewels
beats.summary: The Beauforts' ball is the great event of the winter, in a ballroom that is used only once a year.

beats.scene: Julius Beaufort and his wife greet guests at the top of the staircase
beats.summary: Archer greets the Beauforts at the head of the stairs and goes into the ballroom to look for May.

beats.scene: Mrs Welland whispers news to old ladies as guests gather round the couple
beats.summary: The engagement is announced, and within minutes the whole ballroom is congratulating Archer and May.

beats.scene: Archer and May waltz together beneath the glittering chandeliers
beats.summary: Archer dances with May, who says very little, and he wonders what lies behind her calm.

beats.scene: Archer stands apart at the edge of the dance floor, watching May
beats.summary: Archer thinks that May has been kept in complete innocence and imagines teaching her to see the world.

beats.scene: Ellen enters the ballroom late in a dark dress as heads turn
beats.summary: Ellen arrives late at the ball, and the room grows quiet as she enters.

beats.scene: Archer crosses the floor and bows over Ellen's hand
beats.summary: Archer crosses the whole floor to greet Ellen warmly, in front of the cold looks of the guests.

beats.scene: Ellen and Archer sit on a sofa in a quiet corner of the ballroom
beats.summary: Ellen tells Archer that New York seems small, and he is drawn by her honesty.

beats.scene: Older ladies whisper behind their fans along the wall of the ballroom
beats.summary: The old ladies whisper behind their fans, and Archer is angry at how cruel good manners can be.

beats.scene: Archer rides home alone in a dark carriage through the winter streets
beats.summary: After the ball Archer rides home alone, happy about May but strangely stirred by Ellen.

beats.scene: Archer's mother and sister sit at breakfast in a neat dining room
beats.summary: The next morning Archer's mother and his sister Janey are delighted by the news of his engagement.

beats.scene: A portrait of Archer's late father hangs above the quiet drawing room fire
beats.summary: Archer's father died long ago, but his rules still govern the household, and life follows the old polite habits.

beats.scene: Mrs Archer pours tea while Janey leans forward to listen
beats.summary: Mrs Archer says she pities Ellen but hopes the engagement will quiet the talk and keep the family respectable.

beats.scene: Old Sillerton Jackson sits at the Archers' dinner table with a napkin tucked in
beats.summary: Old Sillerton Jackson dines with the Archers and loves to talk about the Countess.

beats.scene: Jackson leans over his plate and lowers his voice at the table
beats.summary: Jackson hints that a secretary left the Count's house at the same time as Ellen, though nothing is proved.

beats.scene: Archer frowns at the dinner table while the others nod
beats.summary: Archer says that nobody at the table knows the truth, and finds that his family thinks it kinder not to ask.

beats.scene: A carriage drives up Fifth Avenue toward a huge house of pale stone
beats.summary: Archer goes to see May's grandmother, Mrs Mingott, in her great house far up Fifth Avenue.

beats.scene: Old Mrs Mingott laughs in a huge armchair by the window of her parlour
beats.summary: Mrs Mingott, vast and fearless, laughs and congratulates Archer on his engagement.

beats.scene: Mrs Mingott waves a small plump hand as she talks about her granddaughter
beats.summary: Mrs Mingott laughs at the gossip, says Ellen is a good girl, and promises that nobody will drive her out.

beats.scene: Mrs Mingott points a ringed finger at Archer and laughs
beats.summary: Mrs Mingott tells Archer not to wait for a long engagement, and he leaves admiring her courage.

beats.scene: Mrs Welland holds a stack of polite refusals with a pale, worried face
beats.summary: Many families refuse the Mingotts' dinner for Ellen, and Mrs Welland is deeply distressed.

beats.scene: Archer speaks earnestly to his mother in the Archers' drawing room
beats.summary: Archer tells his mother that only the van der Luydens can change the town's mind about Ellen.

beats.scene: A tall, solemn house on a quiet street where the van der Luydens live
beats.summary: The van der Luydens, Mrs Archer's cousins, are the most respected couple in New York.

beats.scene: Archer and his mother face the van der Luydens in a stiff drawing room
beats.summary: Archer and his mother visit the van der Luydens and explain Ellen's position with great care.

beats.scene: Henry van der Luyden frowns by the fire with his hands behind his back
beats.summary: Henry hesitates, since he has never meddled in the affairs of other families.

beats.scene: Louisa van der Luyden speaks softly to her husband, a letter in her lap
beats.summary: Louisa reminds Henry that the Duke of St Austrey will soon dine with them and suggests inviting Ellen.

beats.scene: Henry van der Luyden nods and takes up a pen at a small desk
beats.summary: Henry agrees, and the van der Luydens write a short note inviting Ellen to dinner.

beats.scene: Ellen in a plain dark gown arrives at the candlelit van der Luyden dinner
beats.summary: On the night of the dinner Ellen arrives and is welcomed by Louisa while the guests watch to learn how they should behave.

beats.scene: The Duke of St Austrey laughs with Ellen across the candlelit table
beats.summary: At dinner the Duke talks warmly with Ellen, and everyone sees that she is accepted.

beats.scene: Ellen and Archer speak quietly in a corner of the drawing room after dinner
beats.summary: After dinner Ellen thanks Archer, having guessed that the invitation was his idea, and he feels an unexpected closeness.

beats.scene: A florist's shop where a box of yellow roses lies open on a counter
beats.summary: Archer orders yellow roses for Ellen, but at the last moment takes back his card.

beats.scene: Archer climbs the steps of a narrow house in a shabby street
beats.summary: Archer calls on Ellen at her small house in an unfashionable street.

beats.scene: A small room full of shaded lamps, Eastern rugs, bronze figures and strange flowers
beats.summary: Ellen's rooms are full of foreign treasures and look like no house that Archer knows.

beats.scene: Ellen pours tea from a small pot as Archer sits down
beats.summary: Ellen gives Archer tea in the European way and says that few of her cousins' friends have called.

beats.scene: Ellen and Archer talk by the window of her sitting room
beats.summary: Ellen says that everyone in New York is kind but that nobody says what they think, and Archer begins to see his world through her eyes.

beats.scene: Yellow roses stand in a tall glass on a small table by the window
beats.summary: Ellen says that yellow roses came without a name, and Archer says nothing.

beats.scene: Ellen speaks of her cousin May with her face turned toward the window
beats.summary: They speak of May, and Ellen praises her warmly while Archer feels proud and a little uneasy.

beats.scene: Archer walks away from Ellen's house along a grey street at dusk
beats.summary: Archer leaves, comparing Ellen's bright rooms with Mrs Welland's heavy drawing room, and walks home slowly.

beats.scene: Sillerton Jackson speaks quietly to Archer in a corner of the club
beats.summary: Archer hears at his club that Beaufort's carriage is often seen at Ellen's door.

beats.scene: Archer sits alone in his study at night with an unread book
beats.summary: Alone at night, Archer tells himself that his interest in Ellen is only kindness to a relation.

beats.scene: Mr Letterblair sits behind a heavy desk in a law office full of papers
beats.summary: Mr Letterblair, the old family lawyer, calls Archer into his private room about a delicate matter.

beats.scene: A letter and a bundle of papers lie on Mr Letterblair's desk
beats.summary: Mr Letterblair says that Ellen wishes for a divorce and shows Archer a letter from the Count.

beats.scene: Archer reads a long letter by lamplight with a troubled face
beats.summary: Archer reads the Count's accusations, which mention the secretary, and feels pity and anger.

beats.scene: Mr Letterblair leans back in his chair and speaks gravely
beats.summary: Mr Letterblair says that a divorce would be printed in every newspaper and would hurt the whole family.

beats.scene: Archer stands at the window of the law office looking down at the street
beats.summary: Archer agrees to speak to Ellen, though he is uneasy about the task.

beats.scene: Archer sits opposite Ellen in her drawing room as she listens quietly
beats.summary: Archer explains to Ellen what a divorce case would mean in New York.

beats.scene: Ellen looks down at her hands, then speaks softly of freedom
beats.summary: Ellen says that she only wanted to be free and does not understand why freedom costs so much here.

beats.scene: Ellen holds out her hand to Archer with a sad, small smile
beats.summary: Ellen gives way and promises to do what the family advises.

beats.scene: Archer walks down the steps of Ellen's house under a pale winter sky
beats.summary: Archer is ashamed of how easily he won, as if he had taken something precious from her.

beats.scene: Mr Letterblair shakes Archer's hand warmly at the door of his office
beats.summary: Mr Letterblair thanks Archer, the family is relieved, and Archer admits that he is falling in love with Ellen.

beats.scene: Snow falls on a New York street outside Archer's office window
beats.summary: As winter deepens the Wellands go south to Florida for Mr Welland's health, and May writes cheerful letters.

beats.scene: Archer sits alone in his club by a window as the snow falls
beats.summary: Archer decides to go to St Augustine and ask May to marry him sooner, hoping marriage will end his doubts.

beats.scene: A train runs south through green pine forests under bright sunlight
beats.summary: Archer travels south by train, leaving the snow behind him.

beats.scene: May in a wide sunhat walks through a garden of palms toward Archer
beats.summary: Archer finds May in a garden, and she is surprised and delighted to see him.

beats.scene: Archer and May walk beside an old Spanish fort with the sea behind them
beats.summary: Archer asks May to marry him in the spring, but she says her family expects a proper long engagement.

beats.scene: Archer speaks earnestly to May on a bench while she shakes her head gently
beats.summary: Archer argues, but May says that it is simply the way things are done, and he sees that she will not be moved.

beats.scene: Mr Welland walks along the shore with a scarf held tight to his throat
beats.summary: Mr Welland talks anxiously of draughts and doctors, and Archer sees how small the Wellands' world is.

beats.scene: May and Archer sit under a tree at sunset as she speaks bravely
beats.summary: May tells Archer that if he loves another woman, he is free to say so.

beats.scene: Archer takes May's hand and shakes his head under the evening sky
beats.summary: Archer denies that there is anyone else, feeling guilty and moved by her honesty.

beats.scene: May waves from a garden gate as Archer drives away toward the station
beats.summary: Archer leaves Florida without an early wedding, uneasy and a little relieved.

beats.scene: Archer reads a letter at his desk; the winter light is thin
beats.summary: Back in New York, Archer finds that Ellen's name is in his thoughts even when he tries not to think of her.

beats.scene: Ellen speaks lightly to Archer in old Mrs Mingott's parlour
beats.summary: Ellen tells Archer that she is going to Boston for a few days, without saying why.

beats.scene: Archer packs a bag by lamplight with a bundle of legal papers beside it
beats.summary: Archer finds a small legal errand that takes him to Boston too.

beats.scene: A Frenchman rises politely among palms and ferns in a glass conservatory
beats.summary: In Boston Archer goes to the house where Ellen is staying and meets a Frenchman, Monsieur Rivière.

beats.scene: Monsieur Rivière sits among the ferns and speaks earnestly
beats.summary: Rivière says that he came from the Count to ask Ellen to return, and that she has refused him.

beats.scene: Rivière lowers his voice and smiles sadly as Archer listens
beats.summary: Rivière admits that it was he who helped Ellen to escape from her husband's house.

beats.scene: Rivière takes his hat at the garden door and bows to Archer
beats.summary: Rivière tells Archer that Ellen is brave and needs good friends, then leaves for Paris.

beats.scene: Ellen walks into the conservatory and sees Archer standing among the palms
beats.summary: Ellen comes in, surprised and glad, and she and Archer walk to the Common and find a bench.

beats.scene: Archer and Ellen sit on a bench under bare trees in the Boston Common
beats.summary: On the bench Ellen says she knows why Archer came, and he does not deny it.

beats.scene: Ellen shakes her head gently on the bench while Archer looks away
beats.summary: Ellen says that they must never hurt May, and Archer returns to New York resolved to marry soon.

beats.scene: The Wellands step down from a train into a crowd of porters
beats.summary: The Wellands return from Florida at the end of the winter, and Archer meets them at the station.

beats.scene: Archer speaks earnestly to Mrs Welland in her heavy, comfortable drawing room
beats.summary: Archer asks Mrs Welland to let him marry May in the spring, and she is shocked.

beats.scene: Mrs Welland sighs and nods while Mr Welland coughs in the corner
beats.summary: Touched by Archer's eagerness, and reminded of Mrs Mingott's wishes, Mrs Welland agrees to a spring wedding.

beats.scene: May laughs and claps her hands in a sunny sitting room
beats.summary: May is delighted by the news, and Archer feels relief together with a strange, dull weight.

beats.scene: Boxes of silver, lace and jewels fill a drawing room table by table
beats.summary: Wedding presents pour into the Wellands' house, each one a sign of New York's approval.

beats.scene: Mrs Archer lifts an old jewel from a velvet case while Janey admires it
beats.summary: Mrs Archer gives May an old family jewel and has it reset in the fashion of the day.

beats.scene: Archer and May stand in the empty rooms of a small new house
beats.summary: Archer and May plan their new house, and May agrees to everything without an opinion of her own.

beats.scene: Young men raise glasses around a long table at Archer's bachelor dinner
beats.summary: Archer's friends give him a bachelor dinner, joking about married life, while he feels strangely far away.

beats.scene: Archer holds a small parcel and a folded note in his study
beats.summary: A small gift arrives from Ellen with a kind note, and Archer holds it for a long time.

beats.scene: Archer lies awake in his dark bedroom on the night before the wedding
beats.summary: On the eve of the wedding Archer lies awake and tells himself that duty is the same as happiness.

beats.scene: Carriages line up outside Grace Church as guests in fine clothes arrive
beats.summary: Grace Church fills with the best of New York, and Mrs Mingott arrives in her great carriage.

beats.scene: May walks up the aisle on her father's arm in a long white veil
beats.summary: May walks toward Archer on her father's arm, radiant in white.

beats.scene: Archer and May stand before the minister at the altar and join hands
beats.summary: Archer and May exchange their vows.

beats.scene: Bells ring as the newly married couple step out of the church into sunshine
beats.summary: The couple leave the church to the sound of bells, and the crowd throws flowers.

beats.scene: Guests raise glasses to the bride and groom at the Wellands' wedding breakfast
beats.summary: At the wedding breakfast at the Wellands' house the guests drink to the couple.

beats.scene: A carriage decorated with ribbons drives away from the Wellands' house
beats.summary: The couple leave for a quiet week in the country before sailing for Europe.

beats.scene: A steamship crosses the grey sea with May and Archer standing at the rail
beats.summary: They sail for Europe, and May enjoys the voyage while Archer's thoughts wander.

beats.scene: May smiles in front of a famous European monument as Archer looks away
beats.summary: On their honeymoon May is cheerful and kind but never curious, and Archer feels how little they share.

beats.scene: Archer reads aloud on a hotel balcony at sunset as May watches the sky
beats.summary: Archer reads poetry to May, but she listens politely and thinks of other things.

beats.scene: A carriage stops before a small new house in the evening light
beats.summary: The couple come home to New York, and Archer enters his own house as a married man.

beats.scene: May arranges flowers in the bright drawing room of the new house
beats.summary: May makes the new house perfect, and Archer sees that she has a gift for order.

beats.scene: Archer works at a heavy desk in the law office among piles of papers
beats.summary: Archer returns to the law office, where the work is dry and respectable and leaves him free to think.

beats.scene: A long dinner table with candles, silver and the van der Luydens as guests
beats.summary: The Archers give their first dinner party, and the van der Luydens honour it with their presence.

beats.scene: Archer sits alone by the fire in his small library at night
beats.summary: After the guests have gone, Archer retires to his library, the only room that is wholly his.

beats.scene: The Wellands and the Archers dine on Sunday with Mr Welland at the head
beats.summary: At the Sunday family dinner Mr Welland talks of his health, and Archer sees the same old conversations repeat.

beats.scene: Archer sees Ellen across a crowded room at old Mrs Mingott's reception
beats.summary: At Mrs Mingott's reception Archer sees Ellen across the room and speaks only politely to her.

beats.scene: May speaks kindly of Ellen at their evening fireside
beats.summary: May says that the family is unfair to Ellen and that they should invite her to dinner, and Archer finds her goodness hard to bear.

beats.scene: May and Archer discuss the summer at the breakfast table over letters
beats.summary: The Wellands will go to Newport for the summer, and Archer agrees to join May there at weekends.

beats.scene: Shuttered houses stand in a hot, empty New York street in June
beats.summary: The city empties in the summer heat, and Archer works alone in the shut-up town.

beats.scene: A train carries Archer through summer fields toward the sea at Newport
beats.summary: At the end of the week Archer takes the train to Newport, where May is waiting.

beats.scene: May stands on a veranda in a pale dress above the sea
beats.summary: At Newport Archer finds May in her family's house by the sea, in a scene of summer beauty.

beats.scene: Carriages drive along a seaside road lined with summer cottages
beats.summary: Newport in summer is simply New York carried to the seaside, with the same families and the same rules.

beats.scene: Striped awnings and targets stand on a wide green lawn at a garden party
beats.summary: A great garden party is held with an archery contest, the fashionable sport of the summer.

beats.scene: Young ladies in white dresses stand in a line and draw their bows
beats.summary: One by one the young ladies shoot, and most of the arrows miss the target.

beats.scene: May draws her bow on the sunny lawn and her arrow strikes the target
beats.summary: May draws her bow with perfect calm, and her arrow hits the very heart of the target.

beats.scene: May receives a prize with a small curtsey while Mrs Welland beams
beats.summary: May wins the archery prize, and Archer is proud as everyone praises his wife.

beats.scene: A woman in a pale dress crosses a bright lawn with a parasol
beats.summary: Ellen arrives very late and alone, walking slowly across the grass toward the awnings.

beats.scene: Ellen kisses May on the cheek beside the target and then turns to Archer
beats.summary: Ellen congratulates May warmly and tells Archer that marriage evidently agrees with him.

beats.scene: Archer watches Ellen sitting alone on a veranda looking at the sea
beats.summary: Archer sees Ellen alone on a veranda and decides to go to her if she turns before a boat passes the lighthouse.

beats.scene: A small white sailboat slides past the lighthouse while Ellen sits motionless
beats.summary: The boat passes the lighthouse, Ellen does not turn, and Archer walks away hurt and ashamed.

beats.scene: Shutters are opened on the great houses of a New York street in autumn
beats.summary: The Archers return to New York in the autumn, and the winter season begins again.

beats.scene: Julius Beaufort leans over Ellen's chair in an opera box
beats.summary: At the opera Archer sees Ellen in the company of Julius Beaufort once more.

beats.scene: Archer paces up and down his small library with his hands behind his back
beats.summary: Archer is jealous and ashamed of it, since a married man has no right to such a feeling.

beats.scene: Old Mr Letterblair frowns at a column of figures in his office
beats.summary: Mr Letterblair quietly tells Archer that he would not leave a penny in Beaufort's bank.

beats.scene: Old gentlemen whisper in the corner of the club over their newspapers
beats.summary: At the club the older men whisper that Beaufort's affairs are not as sound as they appear.

beats.scene: Anxious crowds gather outside the doors of a bank on a grey morning
beats.summary: A rumour runs through the streets that Beaufort's bank cannot pay its debts.

beats.scene: Beaufort stands alone in an empty bank office as the last clerks leave
beats.summary: Beaufort's bank closes and he is ruined, left alone in his empty office.

beats.scene: The Beauforts' great house stands dark with its shutters closed
beats.summary: Society turns against the Beauforts; their house stands dark and nobody calls.

beats.scene: Regina Beaufort in a plain black dress speaks earnestly to an old lady
beats.summary: Regina Beaufort asks her relatives to stand by her, but they refuse to help her husband.

beats.scene: May speaks gravely beside the lamp while Archer listens in silence
beats.summary: May says that she pities Regina but that the family must be firm, and Archer wonders whether her certainty is admirable or terrible.

beats.scene: Relatives in black hurry up the steps of old Mrs Mingott's great house
beats.summary: Old Mrs Mingott has a stroke, and the family hurries to her house, though her mind remains clear.

beats.scene: Ellen sits beside the huge bed and holds the old lady's hand
beats.summary: Ellen comes to live in the great house and nurses her grandmother day and night.

beats.scene: Archer stands in a hushed hall as Ellen comes down the stairs
beats.summary: Archer goes to ask after the old lady and meets Ellen alone for the first time in months.

beats.scene: Ellen and Archer talk in a small sitting room beside the grand staircase
beats.summary: Ellen says that she pities Regina and that Beaufort was merely a friend who talked of the wider world.

beats.scene: Ellen smiles at Archer at the door of the great house
beats.summary: Ellen tells Archer that she sometimes walks in the Metropolitan Museum because it is the only quiet place in town.

beats.scene: Archer walks into a long, almost empty museum room lined with glass cases
beats.summary: Archer goes to the Metropolitan Museum and finds its rooms almost empty and silent.

beats.scene: Ellen stands before a glass case of old cups and carved figures
beats.summary: Archer finds Ellen before a glass case, and she says that nothing is so restful as forgotten things.

beats.scene: Archer speaks passionately to Ellen among the glass cases
beats.summary: Archer tells Ellen that he loves her and cannot go on pretending.

beats.scene: Ellen shakes her head with tears in her eyes between the glass cases
beats.summary: Ellen says that she cannot build her happiness on May's pain, and that there is no place where they could go.

beats.scene: Archer and Ellen stand on the museum steps in the cold grey light
beats.summary: They leave the museum with nothing decided, and Archer is astonished that his whole life has changed.

beats.scene: Archer sits at his law desk staring at a page without reading
beats.summary: After the museum Archer cannot work, and May kindly notices that he looks tired.

beats.scene: A folded note lies beside Archer's plate at the breakfast table
beats.summary: A note comes from Ellen, who is visiting Washington, asking Archer to meet her train on Thursday.

beats.scene: A ferry boat crosses a dark river at dusk with yellow lamps glowing
beats.summary: On Thursday evening Archer crosses the river by ferry to meet Ellen's train.

beats.scene: Ellen steps from the train in a dark travelling cloak with a small bag
beats.summary: Ellen steps off the train looking tired, and her face lights up when she sees him.

beats.scene: Archer and Ellen sit close together in the dark closed carriage
beats.summary: In the closed carriage Archer takes Ellen's hand, and she does not take it away.

beats.scene: Street lamps slide past the carriage window as Ellen speaks quietly
beats.summary: Ellen says that she will not be Archer's secret love, a life she has seen in Europe.

beats.scene: Ellen turns her pale face toward Archer in the dim light of the carriage
beats.summary: Ellen says that she can only love Archer by giving him up.

beats.scene: Archer leans forward in the dark and speaks fiercely to Ellen
beats.summary: Archer protests that they are sacrificing their lives, but Ellen will not build her new life on May's pain.

beats.scene: The carriage stops before Mrs Mingott's great house with a single lamp lit
beats.summary: The carriage reaches the great house, and Ellen steps down without looking back.

beats.scene: Archer walks alone through a quiet avenue at night with his collar turned up
beats.summary: Archer walks home alone, understanding her reasons but unable to accept that the story must end here.

beats.scene: Ellen in a travelling cloak speaks to Archer in a quiet hallway
beats.summary: Ellen tells Archer that she has decided to go back to Europe, with an allowance from her grandmother.

beats.scene: Archer takes both of Ellen's hands in the hallway and looks into her face
beats.summary: Archer says that he will follow her to Europe, and Ellen says that he must not.

beats.scene: Archer sits at his library desk at night with a blank sheet of paper
beats.summary: Archer plans what he will say to May: the whole truth and a plea to be set free.

beats.scene: Archer opens the drawing room door and sees May sewing beside a lamp
beats.summary: Archer comes home early to speak and finds May sewing quietly with a strange new light in her face.

beats.scene: May smiles shyly beside the lamp and speaks softly to Archer
beats.summary: Before Archer can speak, May tells him that she is expecting a baby.

beats.scene: Archer kneels beside May's chair and holds her hands
beats.summary: Archer kneels in silence, and May says that she told Ellen about the baby two weeks ago.

beats.scene: Archer sits perfectly still while the lamp burns on the table beside him
beats.summary: Archer understands that Ellen already knew about the child on the night of the carriage, and said nothing.

beats.scene: Archer sits alone in his library at night with his head in his hands
beats.summary: Late that night Archer knows that he cannot leave a wife who is to be a mother, and the door he meant to open is closed.

beats.scene: Two grandmothers embrace in a drawing room with tears of happiness
beats.summary: Both families rejoice at the news, and Archer feels the walls of his life moving closer.

beats.scene: May speaks beside the lamp with a shy smile about a dinner party
beats.summary: May tells Archer that Ellen is going back to Europe and that she wishes to give a farewell dinner for her.

beats.scene: May writes invitations at her small desk in her neat upright hand
beats.summary: May sends invitations to the farewell dinner, and this time every family accepts.

beats.scene: A long table with candles, flowers and silver is ready for the family dinner
beats.summary: On the night of the dinner the whole clan gathers: the van der Luydens, the Mingotts and the Wellands.

beats.scene: Ellen enters in a pale gown and stands calmly among the relatives
beats.summary: Ellen arrives last, calm and gracious, as the guest of honour.

beats.scene: Guests raise their glasses to Ellen around the long candlelit table
beats.summary: Throughout the dinner the family speaks warmly of Ellen's return to Europe, where they agree she belongs.

beats.scene: Archer looks down a long table at the smiling faces of the family
beats.summary: Archer looks along the table and sees the same careful, watchful expression on every face.

beats.scene: Archer sits very still as he understands what the whole family has done
beats.summary: Archer realises that the whole family has known about his feeling for Ellen and has worked together, in silence, to keep them apart.

beats.scene: May smiles at Archer from the far end of the table with perfect sweetness
beats.summary: Archer wonders how much May knows and how much of the evening was her design.

beats.scene: Ellen puts on her cloak in the hall and holds out a gloved hand
beats.summary: In the hall Ellen says goodbye to Archer in the same polite words she gives to everyone, but her hand stays in his a moment longer.

beats.scene: Ellen steps into a carriage in the evening and drives away down the street
beats.summary: Ellen leaves in her carriage, and Archer lets her go without a word.

beats.scene: Archer closes the front door as May waits in the lamplit hall
beats.summary: Archer goes back in, and May says that dear Ellen looked lovely, and he agrees because there is nothing else to say.

beats.scene: Archer holds a newborn baby while May smiles from her pillows
beats.summary: May gives birth to a son, Dallas, and Archer holds the tiny child with wonder.

beats.scene: Archer carries small Dallas on his shoulders along a park path on a Sunday
beats.summary: Dallas becomes the chief delight of Archer's life, and the boy asks questions that no one in the older generation would dare to ask.

beats.scene: May sits with three young children in a sunny parlour full of toys
beats.summary: Two more children follow, and May is a devoted and tireless mother.

beats.scene: Archer sits at a committee table among serious men, his hair now grey
beats.summary: Years pass, and Archer becomes a respected citizen who works patiently for honest government.

beats.scene: A tall new building rises beside an old brownstone house on a busy street
beats.summary: New York changes quickly, with new money, new buildings and new manners, and the old families begin to fade.

beats.scene: Relatives in black stand in a hushed room around a great bed
beats.summary: One by one the old people die, and among them the great Mrs Mingott, who meets the end with courage.

beats.scene: Archer sits at his library desk at night beside a locked drawer
beats.summary: Archer never writes to Ellen or speaks of her, but keeps the memory in a private room of his mind.

beats.scene: Dallas, now a tall young man, laughs and talks freely at the family table
beats.summary: Dallas grows into a frank, cheerful young man, and Archer marvels at how freely he speaks.

beats.scene: May sits beside a sick child's bed with a cool cloth in the lamplight
beats.summary: One winter May nurses a sick child through long nights, and she catches the fever herself.

beats.scene: Archer stands bareheaded beside a grave on a grey winter day with his children
beats.summary: May dies, and Archer mourns her sincerely, honouring her for what she was.

beats.scene: Archer sits alone in his quiet library, a grey-haired widower with a book
beats.summary: More years go by, and Archer lives alone in the quiet house, a widower content without being fulfilled.

beats.scene: Dallas speaks cheerfully to his father about his wedding plans
beats.summary: Dallas tells his father that he is going to marry Fanny Beaufort, the daughter of the once-disgraced banker.

beats.scene: Archer listens thoughtfully as his son talks happily about Fanny
beats.summary: Dallas says that nobody cares about the old rules any more, and Archer thinks how different his own generation was.

beats.scene: Dallas shows his father two steamship tickets across a library table
beats.summary: Dallas suggests a last holiday together in Europe before the wedding, and Archer agrees after some hesitation.

beats.scene: Archer and Dallas walk beside a river in Paris in the bright afternoon
beats.summary: In Paris Archer sees again the city he has avoided, more beautiful and more painful than he remembered.

beats.scene: Dallas speaks lightly at a cafe table while Archer stirs his coffee
beats.summary: Over coffee Dallas says that he has arranged to visit Countess Olenska the next afternoon.

beats.scene: Dallas speaks gently to his father at a table outside a cafe
beats.summary: Dallas says that before she died his mother told him that Archer once gave up what he most wanted, when she asked him.

beats.scene: Archer stops in a Paris street with his hat in his hand
beats.summary: Archer realises that May knew everything, said nothing and was generous to the end.

beats.scene: Dallas walks beside his father, looking at him kindly on a sunny street
beats.summary: Dallas asks whether Ellen was the woman Archer gave up, and Archer answers truthfully that she was.

beats.scene: Archer stands at a hotel window at night watching Paris lamps glow
beats.summary: That night Archer cannot sleep, wondering whether Ellen has changed and whether she remembers.

beats.scene: Archer and Dallas cross a sunny Paris street toward a great golden dome
beats.summary: The next afternoon Archer and Dallas walk toward the Countess's home, near the golden dome of the Invalides.

beats.scene: A wide, quiet Paris square with trees, benches and tall pale houses
beats.summary: They come to a wide, quiet square near the Countess's building, and Archer's legs grow heavy.

beats.scene: Dallas points up at a high balcony of a tall building in the square
beats.summary: Dallas points to the Countess's high balcony, and Archer stops in the square and cannot go on.

beats.scene: Dallas turns in surprise to his father, who shakes his head slowly
beats.summary: Dallas asks why his father has stopped, and Archer says that he does not think he will go up.

beats.scene: Archer sits alone on a bench at the edge of a Paris square
beats.summary: Archer sits on a bench and tells Dallas to go up without him, saying that his father is old-fashioned.

beats.scene: Dallas enters the tall building while Archer watches the balcony from the bench
beats.summary: Dallas goes into the building, and Archer watches the balcony and counts the moments.

beats.scene: Archer imagines Ellen rising in a room of soft lamps high above the square
beats.summary: Archer imagines the room above the balcony, with Ellen rising to open the door to his son.

beats.scene: Archer sits perfectly still on the bench, looking up at the sunlit window
beats.summary: Archer feels that Ellen is more real to him on the bench than she would be if he went up.

beats.scene: A servant closes the shutters of the balcony as the light begins to fade
beats.summary: A servant closes the shutters of the balcony, and Archer understands that the visit is over.

beats.scene: Archer walks alone down a Paris street toward his hotel at dusk
beats.summary: Archer walks back alone to his hotel through the Paris evening, and the age of innocence cannot be returned to.

B1B2: On a winter evening long ago in New York, Newland Archer walks into the Academy of Music after the singing has begun. Fashion says that a gentleman should never arrive on time, so he is not worried.
In the family box he sees May Welland, the young woman he is going to marry. She is dressed all in white and holds a bunch of lilies of the valley.

Beside May sits a slender woman with dark hair, wearing a gown that is plainer than fashion allows. She is May's cousin Ellen, Countess Olenska, who has come home to New York after many years in Europe.

In the club box, Lawrence Lefferts and old Sillerton Jackson are whispering about the Countess. Everyone knows that she has left her husband, a rich Polish count, and run away from his house in Europe.
The old families of New York hate any kind of scandal, and they would rather say nothing than tell the truth. Archer can see that they are afraid Ellen will bring trouble to them all.
Archer feels sorry for May and her family, who are being stared at by the whole house. He decides to announce his engagement tonight, so that everyone will see that the Wellands are not alone.
As he walks round the theatre, Archer thinks about the months in which he has waited. May's family, who like to do everything correctly, have made him keep the secret until the proper moment.
Archer opens the door of the box and bows to May's mother and aunt. May turns to him with a smile that makes him feel that nothing in the world could be wrong.
Ellen holds out her hand and says that she remembers him from long ago. They knew each other as children, she tells him, and Archer finds that he can just remember her too.
Archer quietly asks May if he may announce their engagement at the Beauforts' ball that night. She looks at her mother, who nods, and May answers him with a blush and a smile.
The Beauforts' house has the finest ballroom in New York, and tonight it shines with lights and flowers. Every family that matters has been invited, and nobody would dream of missing the party.
At the top of the stairs Archer greets Julius Beaufort and his wife Regina, who smile at every guest in the same way. Then he goes into the ballroom, hoping to find May.
Mrs Welland whispers the news to two old ladies, and within ten minutes the whole ballroom knows. People crowd round Archer and May to shake hands and to kiss May's cheek.
Archer and May dance under the great chandeliers, and she smiles at all their friends. She says very little, and he wonders what she is really thinking behind her calm eyes.
Archer thinks that May has been brought up to know nothing at all about life. He would like to teach her to think for herself, but he suspects that her family would never allow it.
Ellen comes into the ballroom long after the dancing has begun. Heads turn, the talk stops for a moment, and several ladies look at each other with raised eyebrows.
Archer sees how cold the faces are, so he crosses the floor to greet her at once. He offers her his arm, and for a moment the two of them stand alone in the middle of the room.

They sit together on a sofa in a quiet corner, and Ellen laughs softly at how small New York seems. She is frank about everything, and Archer is surprised to find that her frankness does not shock him.
Along the walls the older ladies are whispering behind their fans, and some of them pretend not to see Ellen. Archer feels angry that people who are so careful about manners can be so unkind.
After the ball Archer rides home through the cold, empty streets. He tells himself that he is happy, because he is engaged to May, but he keeps thinking about Ellen.

The next morning Archer tells his mother and his sister Janey about the engagement, though they have already heard it. They are delighted, and Mrs Archer says that May is a girl of the very best family.
Archer's father died many years ago, but his rules still govern the house. Meals are served at the same hours, the same cousins are invited, and nobody ever asks why.

Mrs Archer says that she feels sorry for poor Ellen, but that a wife should not leave her husband. She hopes that Newland's engagement will quiet the talk and make the Mingotts look respectable again.
That evening old Sillerton Jackson comes to dinner at the Archers' house, as he often does. He knows the secrets of every family in New York, and he cannot resist telling them over a good meal.

Jackson lowers his voice and says that there was a secretary in the Count's house. Some people say that Ellen ran away with him, though nobody can prove it, and Jackson raises his eyebrows meaningfully.
Archer says that nobody at the table knows what really happened in the Count's house. His mother answers gently that it is better not to ask, and Jackson smiles into his wine.

The next day Archer goes to see May's grandmother, old Mrs Mingott, who lives in a huge house far up Fifth Avenue. Years ago she built it there in a part of the city that the best families thought too far out.

Mrs Mingott sits in an armchair so large that she can hardly move, and she laughs loudly when Archer comes in. She tells him that he and May make a pretty couple, and that the Welland family is lucky to have him.
Mrs Mingott laughs at the gossips and calls them cowards. She says that Ellen is a good girl who has had bad luck, and that nobody in her family will turn her out.
Before he goes, Mrs Mingott tells him not to wait for a long engagement. She says that she wants to see the wedding while she is alive, and Archer leaves the house admiring her courage.
The Mingotts invite many families to a dinner for Ellen, but most of them refuse politely. Mrs Welland shows the little notes to Archer, and her hands are shaking.
Archer tells his mother that the families will change their minds only if the van der Luydens support Ellen. Mrs Archer is shocked by the idea, but she does not say no.
Henry and Louisa van der Luyden are cousins of Mrs Archer, and they are the most respected couple in New York. They live so quietly that people feel honoured whenever they appear at a party.
Archer and his mother explain Ellen's difficulty to the van der Luydens in their grand drawing room. Henry listens with a stern face, and Louisa folds her thin hands.

Henry van der Luyden says slowly that he has never liked to meddle in the affairs of other families. He asks whether the Countess's relations really wish for his help, and he looks as if he would like to refuse.
Louisa van der Luyden speaks softly and reminds her husband that the Duke of St Austrey is soon to dine with them. She suggests that they should ask the Countess to meet him.
At last Henry agrees, and Louisa writes a short note inviting Ellen to dinner. Everyone in New York will hear of the invitation, and it will do more than a hundred arguments.
On the night of the dinner Ellen arrives in a plain dark dress, and Louisa greets her kindly. The other guests watch closely, because they want to see how they ought to behave.
The Duke of St Austrey, a cheerful guest, talks warmly with Ellen across the candlelit table. Everyone sees how pleased the great man is, and nobody dares to look cold any more.
After dinner Ellen finds Archer in the drawing room and thanks him quietly. She has guessed that the invitation was his idea, and he feels a closeness that he cannot explain.
Archer goes to a florist and orders a box of yellow roses to be sent to Ellen. At the last moment he takes back the card, and he does not understand why.
Ellen has rented a small house in a street where actors and artists live. Archer goes to see her one afternoon, though he is not sure that a gentleman should call alone.
Inside, the rooms are lit by soft lamps and filled with foreign treasures. There are Eastern rugs, small tables and flowers in strange vases, and nothing looks like the houses of his friends.
Ellen pours tea into small cups, in the way that she learned in Europe, and says that she is glad he has come. She tells him that few people from the old families have visited her.
Ellen says that everyone in New York is kind to her, but that nobody ever says what they really think. Archer laughs, and then he realises that he cannot disagree with her.
On a table Archer sees the yellow roses he sent, and Ellen says that they came without a name. She looks at him with a small smile, and he says nothing.
They talk about May, and Ellen praises her warmly. She says that May is kind and honest, and Archer feels proud and a little uneasy at the same time.
When Archer leaves, he thinks of the strange, bright rooms he has seen. They make Mrs Welland's heavy drawing room seem like a museum, and he walks home more slowly than usual.
At his club, old Sillerton Jackson tells Archer that Julius Beaufort's carriage is often seen at Ellen's door. He says it lightly, as if it means nothing, but Archer feels a small shock.
That night Archer sits alone in his study with a book that he cannot read. He tells himself that his interest in Ellen is only the kindness that a man owes to his future cousin.
One morning old Mr Letterblair, the family lawyer, calls Archer into his private office. He says that there is a delicate matter, and that Archer will soon be a member of the family.
Mr Letterblair tells Archer that Ellen wants to divorce her husband. He lays a bundle of papers on the desk, among them an angry letter from the Count.
Archer reads the Count's letter, which accuses Ellen of many things, including a friendship with his secretary. He does not believe it, but he sees how much harm it could do if it were made public.
Mr Letterblair says that a divorce case would be printed in every newspaper, and that the whole family would suffer. He believes that Ellen would be happier if she stayed married and lived quietly.
Archer agrees to speak to Ellen, because Mr Letterblair asks him and because he wants to protect her. Still, he leaves the office with a feeling that he has agreed to something unwise.
Archer visits Ellen again, and he explains what a divorce would mean in New York. He says that her private life would be written about in the newspapers, and that her friends would suffer too.
Ellen says that she only wants to be free, and that she does not understand why freedom should cost so much here. She looks at him, and he sees that she is very tired.
In the end, after a long silence, Ellen gives way to him. She says that she trusts him and will do as the family wishes, and she holds out her hand to say goodbye.
Outside, Archer should be pleased with his success, but he is not. He feels ashamed, as if he has taken something precious from her without giving anything in return.
Mr Letterblair thanks Archer warmly, and the whole family is relieved. That night Archer admits to himself that he is falling in love with Ellen, and he knows that it is both wonderful and terrible.
As winter deepens, the Wellands go south to Florida for Mr Welland's health, as they do every year. May writes cheerful letters, and Archer finds that he reads them without much feeling.
Archer decides to travel to St Augustine and ask May to marry him sooner. He tells himself that he is simply in love, but a part of him hopes that marriage will end his doubts.
Archer takes the long train south, and the snow gives way to green pine trees and warm sunshine. By the time he reaches Florida he has taken off his heavy coat.
May is standing in a sunny garden when Archer arrives. She is surprised and delighted, and she comes toward him with both hands held out.
Archer walks with May near the old Spanish fort and asks her to marry him in the spring. She smiles and says that her family expects a proper engagement, with time to prepare everything.
Archer argues that they have no reason to wait, but May answers that it is simply the way things are done. He realises that she is perfectly kind and perfectly immovable.
Mr Welland walks beside the sea with his scarf wrapped tightly round his neck. He talks all afternoon about draughts and doctors, and Archer sees how small the Wellands' world is.
May says quietly that she wants to tell him something. If he has ever loved another woman, or if he does now, she says, she would never hold him to his promise.
Archer takes her hand and tells her that there is no one else. He means to be truthful, but he feels guilty, because the words are not the whole truth.
A few days later Archer takes the train north without winning an earlier wedding. He tells himself that it is not important, but in his heart he is troubled.
Back in New York, Archer works hard at the office, and he goes to dinners and to the club. Yet whenever he is quiet, the thought of Ellen returns, and he cannot drive it away.
One afternoon, at old Mrs Mingott's house, Ellen tells Archer that she is going to Boston for a few days. She does not say why, and Archer is surprised by his own disappointment.

The organ begins, and May walks slowly up the aisle on her father's arm. She is dressed in white, with a long veil, and she looks like a girl in a dream.

The bells ring as Archer and May walk out of the church into the spring sunshine. People throw flowers, and their friends cheer as they step into the carriage.

The Archers give their first grand dinner, and even the van der Luydens come to it. Louisa tells May that she is perfect, and May blushes with pleasure.
After the guests have gone, Archer goes to his small library and shuts the door. It is the only room in the house that is entirely his, and he feels almost like himself there.

At a reception at old Mrs Mingott's house, Archer sees Ellen across the room. They speak only a few polite words, and he sees that she looks tired but calm.
At home May says that the family has been unfair to Ellen, and that they should invite her to dinner more often. Archer thanks her, and finds her kindness almost hard to bear.

At the end of the week Archer takes the train to Newport, where May is waiting. The sea air is cool and fresh after the heat of the city, and he feels his spirits rise.
At Newport, Archer finds May on the veranda of the Wellands' house, which looks out at the sea. She wears a pale summer dress, and the whole place smells of salt and roses.

One by one the young ladies step forward and shoot their arrows at the target. Most of them miss, and the audience claps politely while some of the gentlemen hide their smiles.
Then May steps forward in her white dress, and everyone is quiet. She draws her bow with calm, steady hands, and her arrow flies straight into the centre of the target.

Just then Archer sees a woman at the far side of the lawn, walking slowly toward the tents. It is Ellen, who has arrived very late, and she walks alone, as if she has all the time in the world.
Ellen congratulates May warmly and kisses her on the cheek. Then she turns to Archer and says that he looks well, and he finds that he cannot think of an answer.
Later Archer sees Ellen sitting alone on a veranda, looking out at the sea. A white sailing boat is moving toward the lighthouse, and he makes a secret promise to himself.

One day Mr Letterblair tells Archer, in a low voice, that he would not leave a penny in Beaufort's bank. He has seen too many handsome houses stand on very weak foundations.
At the club the older men whisper that Julius Beaufort's affairs are not as sound as they seem. Beaufort still drives the finest horses in New York, and nobody dares to say it aloud.
