May says that she is very sorry for poor Regina, but that the family must be firm. Archer sees that her sense of right is complete, and that it leaves no room for mercy.
Soon afterward old Mrs Mingott has a stroke, and the whole family hurries to her great house. She is very ill, but her mind is as clear as ever, and she asks for Ellen.
Ellen leaves her small house and comes to nurse her grandmother day and night. The old lady will have nobody else near her, and the family begins to see Ellen in a new light.
Archer goes to the great house to ask after the old lady, and Ellen comes down the stairs to speak to him. They have not been alone together for months, and the hall is very quiet.
Ellen says that she is sorry for Regina Beaufort, and that she saw Beaufort only because he talked of the wider world. Archer feels his jealousy melt away, and he is ashamed that he ever felt it.
As he leaves, Ellen tells Archer that she sometimes escapes to the Metropolitan Museum, the only quiet place in town. She does not ask him to come, but he understands what she means.
On the day they have in mind, Archer goes to the Metropolitan Museum. The long rooms are almost empty, and his steps echo among the glass cases of ancient things.
He finds Ellen standing in front of a glass case of ancient objects, in a dark dress and a small hat. She turns and smiles, and says that old forgotten things are better company than living people.
At last Archer can hold back no longer, and he tells Ellen that he loves her. He says that he made a terrible mistake in marrying, and that he cannot go on pretending.
Ellen says that she cannot build her own happiness on May's pain, and that she will not run away. When Archer begs her to go with him, she asks sadly where in the world they could go.
They leave the museum together, but they decide nothing at all. Outside the winter light is grey, and Archer feels that his whole life has been changed by a talk among old cups.
After the museum Archer finds that he cannot work, and he stares at the same page for an hour. At home May notices that he looks tired and tells him that he should rest.
A short note arrives from Ellen, who has gone to Washington for a few days. She says that she will come back on Thursday, and she asks Archer to meet her at the ferry.
On Thursday evening Archer crosses the river by ferry to meet Ellen's train. The water is black, the lamps are yellow, and his heart is beating hard.
Ellen steps off the train in a dark travelling cloak, tired from her journey. When she sees him her face lights up, and for a moment neither of them speaks.
In the dark carriage they sit close together, and Archer takes her hand. They ride in silence for a long time, listening to the wheels rattle over the stones.
Ellen says that she knows what it is to be a secret love, because she has seen such lives in Europe. She will not live in hotels and hidden rooms, and she will not be that kind of woman.
Ellen says that she can only keep Archer's love by giving him up. If she took what he offers, she says, they would both become smaller, and the love would turn into something ordinary and sad.
Archer protests that they are throwing away their lives to please people who do not love them. He says that May's peace is built on a lie, but Ellen will not hurt May.
At last the carriage stops before Mrs Mingott's great house, where one lamp is burning. Ellen presses his hand once, steps down and goes in without looking back.
Archer walks home alone through the cold streets, thinking of everything that Ellen has said. He understands her reasons, but he cannot make himself believe that the story must end like this.
A few days later Ellen tells Archer, in the quiet hall of Mrs Mingott's house, that she will go back to Europe. Her grandmother has promised her enough money to live on.
Archer tells her that he will follow her to Europe, and that no rule of society can stop him. Ellen says only that he must not, but she does not take her hands away.
That night Archer sits in his library and plans what he will say to May. He wants to tell her the truth honestly and to ask her to forgive him.
The next evening Archer comes home early, determined to speak. He finds May sewing quietly by the lamp, and she looks up at him with a small, shy smile.
Before he can speak, May says softly that she has something to tell him. The doctor was here today, she says, and in a few months they will have a child.
Archer kneels beside her chair and holds her hands, unable to speak. May adds that she told Ellen about the baby two weeks ago, though she was not quite certain then.
Archer understands that Ellen already knew about the baby on the night in the carriage. She refused him knowing it, and she did not say a single word.
Late that night Archer sits alone in his library and knows that he cannot leave a wife who is going to be a mother. The door that he hoped to open is closed, and he feels sad and strangely calm.
Within a day both families know the news, and the grandmothers cry with happiness. Mrs Archer fetches the old family cradle, and Janey begins to knit tiny clothes.
A few days later May tells him that Ellen is going back to Europe. She wishes to give a farewell dinner, and the whole family must come to show how much they love her.
May writes the invitations to the farewell dinner in her neat hand. This time nobody refuses, though the same families once refused to dine with Ellen.
On the night of the dinner the whole clan gathers in the Archers' drawing room. The van der Luydens, the Mingotts and the Wellands are all there, in their finest clothes.
Ellen arrives last, in a pale dress with a thin ribbon at her throat, and she looks calm and beautiful. May kisses her warmly and leads her to the place of honour at the table.
Throughout the dinner the whole family is kind to Ellen, and they speak warmly of her return to Europe. Everyone agrees that she is going home, and they nod as if it were the best news in the world.
Archer looks down the long table at the smiling faces of his family. Every one of them wears the same careful expression, and he begins to feel that something is wrong.
At last Archer understands what the whole evening really means. The whole family knows about his feelings for Ellen, and they have worked together without a word to keep them apart.
From the end of the table May smiles at him with perfect sweetness. He wonders how much she knows, and whether her kindness has been a kind of weapon all this time.
In the hall Ellen puts on her cloak and says goodbye to Archer in the same polite words that she uses for everyone. But her hand stays in his for one moment longer than politeness requires.
Ellen steps into the carriage at the door, and the horses move off into the evening. Archer stands on the step and watches the lamps grow small, and he does not say a word.
Archer goes back into the house, where May is waiting with a gentle smile. She says that dear Ellen looked lovely tonight, and he agrees with her, because there is nothing else that he can say.
In the spring May has a baby boy, and they call him Dallas. Archer holds the tiny child in his arms and is surprised by how much he loves him.
As Dallas grows, he becomes the great joy of Archer's life, and they walk together in the park on Sundays. The boy asks a hundred questions that nobody in the family would ever dare to ask.
Two more children are born, a girl and then another boy, and the house is soon noisy and full. May is a devoted mother, who teaches them to be honest and kind and to behave well.
The years pass, and Archer becomes a respected citizen. He sits on committees for good causes and works for honest government, and his hair turns grey.
New York changes quickly in those years, as new money and new buildings arrive. The old families begin to fade, although they do not like to admit it, and the old rules are slowly forgotten.
One by one the old people of his world die, and among them is the great Mrs Mingott. She faces the end as she faced everything, with courage, and Archer feels that a whole age is closing.
Archer never writes to Ellen, and he never goes to Europe to find her. But he keeps the memory of her in a small room of his mind to which he alone has the key.
Dallas grows into a tall, cheerful young man who says exactly what he thinks. Archer is amazed and delighted, because the boy's frankness is something that his own generation never knew.
One winter May nurses a sick child day and night. She catches the fever herself, and although the doctors try everything, she grows weaker every hour.
May dies, and Archer stands beside her grave on a grey day with his three children. He is surprised by how deeply he mourns, because she was a good wife in every way.
Years go by, and Archer lives alone in the quiet house, a widower with grey hair. His children have grown up, and he fills his evenings with books and old memories.
One day Dallas tells his father that he is going to marry Fanny Beaufort, the daughter of Julius Beaufort. Archer smiles at the irony, because the old scandal is forgotten.
Dallas says that nobody cares about the old rules any more. Archer thinks that his own generation could never have said such a thing, and he presses his son's shoulder.
Dallas suggests that the two of them take a last trip to Europe before the wedding. Archer has not crossed the ocean for many years, and he hesitates, and then he says yes.
In Paris Archer and Dallas walk beside the river in the soft afternoon light. Archer has not seen the city for years, and it is more beautiful than he remembers.
Over coffee Dallas says, in an easy voice, that he has arranged to visit Countess Olenska tomorrow afternoon. Archer's hand stops, and he asks how his son knows where she lives.
Dallas says gently that his mother told him something before she died. She said that Archer once gave up the thing he wanted most in the world, when she asked him to.
Archer walks along a Paris street, and he stops with his hat in his hand. He understands that May knew everything, and that she never said a word.
Dallas asks kindly whether Ellen was the woman his father gave up. Archer says that she was, and that in his day people did not throw away everything for the sake of one love.
That night in the hotel Archer cannot sleep, and he stands at the window watching the lights of Paris. He wonders whether Ellen has changed, and whether she remembers him.

The next afternoon Archer and Dallas walk through the bright streets toward the Invalides, where the great golden dome shines in the sun. Dallas talks cheerfully about buildings and weddings, but Archer says very little.

They come at last to a wide, quiet square with trees and benches, where the tall houses stand in the afternoon sun. Dallas says that the Countess lives somewhere here, and Archer's legs feel suddenly heavy.
Dallas stops and points up at a high balcony with a striped sunshade. That is the place, he says, and Archer stands still in the middle of the square and cannot go on.
Dallas asks his father why he has stopped, and whether he is ill. Archer says that he is quite well, but that he does not think he will go up after all.
Archer sits down on a bench at the edge of the square and tells Dallas to go up without him. He says that Dallas may tell the Countess that his father is old-fashioned, and that this is enough.
Dallas crosses the square and goes into the tall building, and the door closes behind him. Archer stays on his bench, looking up at the balcony with its striped sunshade.
On the bench Archer imagines the room above the balcony, full of soft lamps and foreign treasures. He pictures Ellen looking up when the door opens, and seeing a young man with his father's eyes.
Archer sits perfectly still, looking up at the window in the sunlight. He feels that Ellen is more real to him here, in his memory, than she could be if he went up the stairs.
At last a servant comes out on the balcony and closes the shutters, as the light begins to fade. Archer understands that the visit is over, and that it is time for him to go.
Archer gets up from the bench and walks back to his hotel alone. The evening lamps of Paris are coming on, and he feels strangely at peace.
C1C2: On a winter evening in the New York of the eighteen-seventies, young Newland Archer strolled into the Academy of Music long after the curtain had risen on the garden scene of Faust. A gentleman of fashion was expected to arrive late, for the opera was less an entertainment than a ceremony, and to come early would have suggested that one had nothing better to do. From the back of the club box he looked out across the glittering horseshoe of the house, and a quiet, proprietary pleasure stole over him.

Across the house, in the box of her family, sat May Welland, the girl whom he was to marry, in a gown of spotless white with a bouquet of lilies of the valley in her lap. She seemed to him the very picture of purity, a creature as candid and unspoiled as the flowers he had sent her that morning. He felt, with a pleasure that was half tenderness and half ownership, that this fresh and trusting girl would soon be wholly his.

Beside May, half hidden by the shadow of the curtain, sat a slender dark-haired woman in a gown of dark blue velvet that was far plainer than the fashion of the day allowed. She was Ellen Olenska, May's cousin, who had lately returned to New York after many years in Europe, and he could only just remember her as a thin, strange child who had been carried away across the sea. All round the house he felt the glasses and the eyes turn toward that box, and he understood that something unusual had come to the opera that night.

In the club box behind him, Lawrence Lefferts and old Sillerton Jackson, who knew the history of every family in New York, were murmuring that the Countess had left her husband and fled from his house in Europe. It was said that the Count was a rich Polish nobleman and that his wife had been very unhappy, though nobody could say with certainty what had really passed between them. In that society a woman who left her husband was a danger to every family she touched, and the story had been whispered through the drawing rooms for weeks.

On the stage the singer was plucking the petals of her daisy and sighing that he loved her, while in the boxes the great families of New York sat very still and said nothing at all. Archer knew how they would meet the scandal, which was to hope that it would go away and to behave as though it had never come. It was a world in which the things that were never said counted for more than the things that were, and in which the most dreaded of all misfortunes was to be talked about.

It struck Archer that the right answer to all this whispering was a bold one, and that the girl in white could provide it. If he were to announce his engagement that very night, the families would see that a young man of the best name stood beside the Wellands and the Mingotts, and the scandal would lose a little of its poison. He rose, murmured a word to his friends, and left the club box with the air of a man who has resolved to do something at once generous and agreeable.

As he walked round the back of the theatre, Archer reflected on the months during which his engagement had been a secret known only to the two families. The Wellands, who did everything with the greatest correctness, had insisted that no announcement should be made before the proper moment, and he had submitted with a good grace. Now it seemed to him that the proper moment had arrived, and that fashionable New York would be unable to resist so charming a piece of news.

He slipped into the box just as the aria ended and bowed over the hand of Mrs Welland, who greeted him with the smile of a lady who approves of everything she has arranged. May herself turned toward him, her face brightening as though a lamp had been lit behind it, and he felt that nothing in the world could be wrong while she looked at him like that. In the shadow beside her, the dark-haired stranger moved her head and regarded him with grave, unembarrassed eyes.

She held out her hand with a simplicity that surprised him, as though there were nothing in her situation that could embarrass anyone, and she said that she remembered him very well. They had known each other as children, she told him, and he found that he could recall a thin, dark little girl whom the family had always spoken of in lowered voices. It was strange to see that child grown into a woman who looked upon the whole shocked theatre with perfect calm.

Bending toward her, Archer asked in a low voice whether he might announce their engagement that night at the Beauforts' ball, where all the world would be gathered to hear it. May glanced at her mother, who gave a small, majestic nod, and then she answered him with a blush and a smile that were a great deal more eloquent than words. He left the box feeling like a man who has done a brave thing, though he could not have said whether he had done it for her sake, for the Countess's, or for his own.

The Beauforts' ball was the great event of the winter, and their ballroom, which stood shut and silent for the rest of the year, blazed that night with candles, hothouse flowers and the jewels of a hundred ladies. Julius Beaufort, the banker who owned it, was not of the oldest families, yet his wealth and his charm had made his house a place that nobody could afford to miss. Archer, arriving among the carriages, felt the old pleasant excitement of belonging to a world that knew exactly what it was doing.

At the head of the staircase Julius Beaufort and his wife stood receiving their guests, he with an easy, mocking assurance and she with the fixed smile of a woman who has said the same words to a thousand people. Archer murmured his greetings, noticing that Beaufort's glance was cool, confident and rather amused. Then he passed on into the glittering ballroom, where his eyes searched the crowd for a single white dress.

Mrs Welland, with the air of a woman who is mentioning something of no importance, let the news fall into the ear of one old lady and then another, and within a quarter of an hour the whole ballroom knew. The company gathered round the young couple to murmur their good wishes, to press May's hand and to remark how perfectly matched they were. Archer, who had longed to be rid of secrecy, found himself nodding and smiling in a fog of congratulation.

They danced together beneath the chandeliers, May moving lightly in his arms and smiling at the friends who nodded to them as they passed. She spoke very little, and her silence seemed to him not shyness but a kind of serene reserve, like the stillness of a sheet of clear water. He wondered, with a curiosity that was almost tender, what lay behind that candid face, and could not tell whether there was anything there that he had not already guessed.

It pleased Archer to think that May had been taught nothing of the world, that she had been guarded from every harsh fact as carefully as a plant in a conservatory. Yet he told himself that after their marriage he would teach her to look at life with open eyes, and that she would become his companion rather than merely his wife. It did not occur to him that the innocence he admired had been made, with great care, by the very people whose rules he sometimes secretly despised.

Ellen Olenska came into the ballroom late, when the dancing was already in full swing, and she paused in the doorway as though she did not know that every eye had turned to her. She wore a dress that was darker and simpler than any other in the room, and she carried herself with an easy grace that nobody in New York could have taught her. A little ripple of whispers ran along the walls, and several ladies exchanged glances in which surprise and disapproval were nicely balanced.

Archer saw the coolness of the faces around her and felt a sudden, generous irritation, so he crossed the whole length of the floor to greet her before anyone else could. He bowed over her hand as warmly as he would have done to the queen of the evening, and offered her his arm with a smile that dared the room to object. For a moment they stood together in an island of silence, while the music played on and the guests pretended to look somewhere else.

They found a sofa in a quiet corner of the ballroom, and Ellen confessed with a low laugh that New York seemed to her a great deal smaller than the city she remembered. She spoke of her return and of her wish to be among her own people again with a frankness that was almost childlike, and she did not once appear to defend herself. Archer, who had expected either tears or defiance, found that he was listening with an interest that he did not quite understand.

Along the walls the ladies of the old families whispered behind their fans, and one or two of them turned their shoulders with a precision that could not have been accidental. It seemed to Archer a strange thing that people so scrupulous in the matter of manners should be capable of such quiet cruelty toward a woman who had done them no harm. He felt, for the first time that evening, a little disloyal to the world that had made him.

It was long past midnight when Archer drove home through the cold and empty streets, with the sounds of the ball still ringing in his ears. He told himself that he was a happy man, betrothed to the loveliest and most trusting girl in New York and applauded by everyone he knew. Yet it was the face of the dark-haired stranger, and not the white one he had come to celebrate, that lingered before him in the shadows of the carriage.

At breakfast the next morning, Archer found that his mother and his sister Janey had already heard everything, for in New York news travelled faster than any carriage. Mrs Archer, a small and gentle lady who held a high opinion of correctness, declared that she was delighted, and Janey, who lived chiefly on the romances of other people, clasped her hands in admiration. In that quiet house, where every day moved to the same unhurried rhythm, the engagement was received like a long-expected and perfectly proper event.

Archer's father had been dead for many years, but his rules still governed the quiet house as the habits of a good clock govern a household. Dinner was served at the same hour, the same cousins were asked at the same seasons, and nobody had ever dreamed of inquiring whether things might be done differently. It was a way of life so perfectly settled that it seemed less like a choice than like the weather.

Over tea, Mrs Archer said gently that she pitied poor Ellen, who had been so strangely brought up, but that a wife who left her husband could hardly expect to be received as though nothing had happened. She hoped that her son's engagement to a Welland would quiet the whispering and show that the family could still be trusted to do the proper thing. Janey listened with her eyes wide and said nothing, which was her usual way of enjoying a scandal.

That evening old Sillerton Jackson came to dinner, as he did whenever the Archers' table promised something good. He was a thin, elderly bachelor with a sharp nose and a prodigious memory, who knew the history of every family in New York and the small secrets of most of its cellars. Over the soup and the fish he gave it as his opinion that the Countess Olenska's return was a matter of the gravest importance.

Jackson lowered his voice, though the servants had left the room, and murmured that there had been a secretary in the Count's household who had disappeared at about the same time as the Countess. Nothing had ever been proved, he said, with the air of a man who believed that a great deal had been proved, and the whole matter had been very painful to her family. Mrs Archer pressed her lips together, and Janey leaned forward so far that she nearly upset her glass.

Archer ventured to say that nobody at the table knew what had really happened in the Count's house, and that it seemed hardly fair to condemn a woman who was not there to speak for herself. His mother answered gently that in such cases it was wiser not to inquire, since the truth, whatever it might be, could only make things worse. He saw that the whole table agreed with her, and he understood that in his family the kindest way of being just was to say nothing.

Old Mrs Mingott lived in a huge house of pale stone, far up Fifth Avenue, in a part of the city where the best families would not have dreamed of settling. She had built it there years before in defiance of everyone, and it stood among its neighbours like a fortress in an empty field. He found her enthroned in an immense armchair by the window, so vast in body that she seemed less a lady than a landscape, with her tiny hands and feet peeping out from the folds of her dress.
