Archer, who was never quite sure whether she was joking, laughed with her and sat down.

The old lady waved a small, plump hand and declared that the gossips were cowards and fools who would swallow any story that was whispered to them over a cup of tea. Ellen, she said, was a good girl who had had bad luck, and so long as Catherine Mingott had breath in her body nobody should drive a Mingott out of New York. She said all this with such cheerful scorn that Archer felt the whole weight of the town's displeasure grow a little lighter.

As he rose to go, the old lady pointed a ringed finger at him and told him not to wait for a long engagement, since she wished to see the wedding while she lived. Archer laughed and promised to do what he could, and as he went down the steps he found that he was humming a tune. It seemed to him that there was more honest courage in that great, laughing woman than in all the correct drawing rooms of the city put together.

The Mingotts sent out invitations to a dinner in honour of Ellen, and one after another the replies came back, polite, regretful and perfectly cold. Mrs Welland, pale with distress, showed the little notes to Archer, who saw that each of them had been written in the same careful tone of reluctant refusal. It was New York's way of passing sentence, without a word of accusation and without the smallest chance of appeal.

Archer reasoned that the families would change their minds only if a higher voice were raised on Ellen's behalf, and he knew that there was just one such voice in New York. If Henry and Louisa van der Luyden were to receive the Countess, nobody else would dare to turn her away, and the whole scandal would be quietly buried. His mother was startled by the boldness of the idea, but she did not say no.

Henry and Louisa van der Luyden, who were cousins of Mrs Archer, stood at the very summit of New York society, and everyone agreed that they were the last of the true aristocracy. They lived in great stillness in a tall house with a solemn staircase, and appeared so seldom in the world that their presence at a party was felt as a kind of blessing. They even looked alike, as though a long and perfect marriage had gradually made them into a single dignified person.

In the solemn drawing room, Archer and his mother laid the matter before the cousins with the delicacy of people handling something very fragile. They said nothing of scandal, only that the Countess Olenska had been a little coldly received and that a small gesture from the van der Luydens might remove the misunderstanding. Henry listened with a stern, unmoving face, while Louisa folded her thin hands and looked at her husband as though waiting to be told what she thought.

Henry van der Luyden replied, after a long and painful silence, that he had never been in the habit of interfering in the affairs of other families, and that he feared a public step might be misunderstood. He inquired whether the Countess's own relations truly wished for his help, and whether it was not rather the business of the Mingotts to settle their difficulties among themselves. It was plain that he would have been very glad to say no and be done with it.

It was Louisa who spoke at last, in her soft, level voice, and reminded her husband that the Duke of St Austrey, their guest from England, was to dine with them in a few days. It would be only natural, she suggested, to ask poor Ellen to the table, since a kind action done quietly was the best kind of all. Henry looked at her for a long moment, and Archer saw the whole matter weighed in a silence as solemn as a court of law.

At last Henry gave a slow nod and declared that the thing should be done, and the invitation was written there and then in Louisa's upright hand. It was a short note, scarcely more than a line, but Archer knew that once it was delivered it would travel from drawing room to drawing room like a proclamation. He thanked his cousins with real feeling, and was rather surprised to find how much he cared about the result.

On the night of the dinner Ellen arrived in a plain dark gown, and Louisa van der Luyden, in her stateliest manner, greeted her with a kiss on the cheek. Every guest in the room watched the scene carefully, for in that society the proper way to treat a person was decided entirely by the way the van der Luydens had already treated her. Within a few minutes the temperature of the room had risen several degrees, and people who had avoided Ellen at the ball were smiling at her over their glasses.

The Duke of St Austrey, a hearty and good-humoured guest who knew nothing of the town's quarrels, talked to Ellen across the candlelit table with every sign of delight. His admiration was worth more than a hundred defences, for in New York nothing is so respectable as to be liked by an English nobleman. Archer, watching from farther down the table, saw the verdict of the room change in the space of a single course.

After dinner Ellen found Archer in the drawing room and thanked him in a low voice, for she had guessed at once whose idea the invitation had been. She did it so simply, and with so little embarrassment, that he felt a sudden warmth that had nothing to do with the pleasure of having succeeded. It was a feeling of intimacy, as if the two of them had shared a secret across a room full of people who knew nothing of it.

A few days later Archer found himself in a florist's shop, ordering a box of yellow roses to be sent to the Countess Olenska as a small token of thanks. At the last moment he took back the card he had written and left the flowers to speak for themselves, though he could not have said what he wished them to say. He walked out into the cold air with the uneasy feeling of a man who has done something more important than he intended.

Ellen had taken a small, narrow house in a street where dressmakers, musicians and other unfashionable people were known to live, and the best families regarded her choice with silent horror. Archer, climbing the steps one afternoon, was not entirely sure that a gentleman engaged to her cousin ought to call there alone. He rang the bell all the same, and found that his heart was beating a little faster than the occasion warranted.

The little drawing room was lit by soft, shaded lamps and furnished with Eastern rugs, small bronze figures and flowers in vases of an odd, unfamiliar shape. It had been arranged with such taste and such evident indifference to the rules that it seemed to belong to another country, where people did exactly as they pleased. Archer, whose own world was full of heavy furniture and framed engravings, stood in the doorway for a moment, struck by the sense that he had gone abroad without leaving New York.

Ellen poured tea into thin cups in the foreign style and told him with a smile that she was glad he had come, since so few of her cousins' friends had ventured to call. She said it without bitterness and without a hint of reproach, in the tone of a woman who has long ago stopped expecting the world to be fair. Archer felt that he had been admitted to a room that was warmer and more honest than any in his mother's house.

Ellen remarked that everyone in New York had been wonderfully kind to her, and yet that nobody seemed ever to say what he really thought, as though there were a silent agreement to pretend that unpleasant things did not exist. Archer laughed, and then discovered with some dismay that he could not honestly contradict her. For the first time in his life he found himself looking at the familiar rules of his world as a foreigner might look at them, from outside and with a little astonishment.

On a small table by the window stood the yellow roses he had sent, arranged in a tall glass with great care. Ellen remarked, looking at him with a faint and thoughtful smile, that they had come without a name and that she would have liked to thank the person who sent them. Archer, who could easily have confessed, felt oddly unwilling to do so, and the silence between them grew very still.

They spoke of May, and Ellen praised her cousin with such warmth and simplicity that Archer's heart swelled with a husband's pride. She called her honest and kind and true, and said that she had never met a girl so entirely without pretence. And yet, as he listened, he was aware of a small, cold uneasiness, like a draught from a window that he had not known was open.

When he left, the street seemed grey and heavy after the colour of those little rooms, and he found that he was walking slowly, as though reluctant to arrive anywhere. He thought of Mrs Welland's drawing room, with its mahogany and its heavy curtains, and it seemed to him as ordered and lifeless as a museum. He was not sure whether what he felt was liberty or disloyalty, only that it was new.

At the club, old Sillerton Jackson remarked, in the tone of a man discussing the weather, that Julius Beaufort's carriage had been seen at the Countess Olenska's door a good many times in the last week. Beaufort was a married man, rich and clever and admired, and nobody who knew him would have thought it a harmless friendship. Archer received the news with outward calm and an inward start of annoyance that surprised him.

That night Archer sat alone in his study, with an unread book open on his knee and the fire sinking in the grate. He told himself that his interest in the Countess was only the kindness that a man owed to the cousin of his future wife, and he repeated this several times as though it were a lesson to be learned. It did not escape him that a person who has to say a thing so often does not entirely believe it.

One morning at the law office, Mr Letterblair, the elderly and cautious lawyer who managed the affairs of half the best families in New York, called Archer into his private room. He closed the door with unusual care and said that a delicate matter had arisen, one that must be settled quietly by a person whom the family trusted. Since Archer was about to become one of the Wellands, he said, nobody could be better fitted for the task.

Mr Letterblair explained, with a heavy sigh, that the Countess wished to be divorced from her husband, and that the family was in a state of terror at the very idea. He laid a bundle of papers on the desk, among them a letter from the Count in which the nobleman declared that he would defend himself and blacken her name. Archer, glancing at the cold, handsome handwriting, felt that he was looking into a part of the world that nobody in New York ever spoke of.

Archer read the Count's letter slowly, and found in it the very accusations that Sillerton Jackson had hinted at over the dinner table, written in the brutal language of an offended husband. He did not believe a word of them, though he could not have said why, and he saw that if they were ever read aloud in a court they would stain Ellen's name for the rest of her life. A cold anger rose in him against the man who had written them, and against a world that expected a woman to bear such things in silence.

Mr Letterblair leaned back and observed gravely that a divorce trial would be reported in every newspaper in the country, and that the Count's accusations, true or false, would be repeated in every drawing room. The Countess, he thought, would be much happier if she were to remain married in name and live quietly under the protection of her family. It was his opinion, and that of the Mingotts, that no woman had ever gained much by being freed at such a price.

Archer agreed to speak to the Countess, partly because Mr Letterblair asked him and partly because he honestly believed that he could protect her from a great misfortune. Yet as he walked out into the grey afternoon, he felt that he had agreed to something not wholly honest, as though he had taken sides in a war he did not understand. He pushed the thought firmly away and walked on toward home, telling himself that duty and kindness were pointing in the same direction.

He called on Ellen again, and with a good deal of embarrassment explained to her what a divorce case would mean in New York, where every detail of a woman's private life would be turned over in public. He said that her husband's lawyers would say terrible things, that the newspapers would repeat them, and that even those who loved her would not be able to protect her from the shame. Ellen listened without interrupting, her face quite still and her hands folded in her lap.

When he had finished, Ellen said very quietly that she had only wanted to be free, and that she did not understand why in a country that talked so much of liberty it should cost a woman so dear. She looked at him with a kind of tired sweetness, as if she knew exactly what he was going to say and had no strength left to argue. Archer felt, for a moment, that he was the one who ought to be pleading for forgiveness.

In the end Ellen gave way, with a small smile that he remembered for years afterward. She said that she trusted him, that she would do whatever the family wished, and that she would not ask for the divorce, and she held out her hand to him with a kind of grave courtesy. It was, he thought, the most generous surrender he had ever witnessed, and he did not feel in the least like a victor.

Out in the street Archer ought to have felt the satisfaction of a man who has carried out a difficult task, but what he felt instead was a heavy shame. He had persuaded her to give up her hope of freedom in the name of a family that had not stood by her, and he had done it so easily that he could not forget the look on her face. It seemed to him that he had been used, along with her, as an instrument of the same cold machinery.

Mr Letterblair shook his hand with real warmth, and within a day the whole family had heard that the dreaded divorce was to be given up and that Archer was the man to thank. He accepted their gratitude with a smile that hurt his face, for he already knew, in the darkness of his own mind, what he had been avoiding for weeks. He was falling in love with Ellen Olenska, and the discovery was at once the most wonderful and the most terrible thing that had ever happened to him.

As the winter deepened, the Wellands travelled south to Florida, where Mr Welland's delicate health, and his terror of draughts, required him to pass the coldest months. May wrote cheerful, affectionate letters about sunshine and sea bathing, in which there was not a single line that Archer could not have predicted. He read them with a dutiful smile and felt, with something like alarm, that they left his heart as quiet as a lake in frost.

Archer resolved, with the suddenness of a man who is afraid of his own thoughts, to travel to St Augustine and persuade May to marry him at once. He told himself that it was a lover's impatience, but in the secret depths of his mind he hoped that an early wedding would put a final lock upon a door that he had begun to fear. He asked Mr Letterblair for leave and was granted it with a benevolent smile.

The long journey south took him through a changing country, where the snow thinned and vanished and the grey of the north gave way to forests of pine and the first soft green of a warmer world. By the time he stepped down at the end of the line he had taken off his heavy coat, and the air that met him smelled of salt, oranges and damp earth. It seemed incredible that the town he had left two days before belonged to the same planet.

He found May in the garden of the house where her family were staying, standing under a wide hat among the palms and the flowering shrubs. She started when she saw him, and then her face lit with a pleasure so simple and so complete that he felt a pang of conscience for all that he had been thinking. She came toward him with both hands held out, quite forgetting the proprieties that her mother would have wished her to observe.

They walked together beside the old Spanish fort, where the sea light fell in long bars across the stones, and Archer asked her to marry him in the spring instead of waiting a year. May smiled at him with the sweetness of a child refusing a sweet, and answered that her family expected a proper engagement, with time for the wedding clothes and the presents. It was said so gently and with such calm conviction that he could not tell where his argument had gone.

He argued that they had no reason to wait, that they loved each other, that nobody in the world would be harmed by an earlier wedding, and May listened with perfect patience. When he had finished, she answered only that it was the way things were done and that she could not see why they should wish to be different from everyone else. He understood that she was as kind as ever and as immovable as a rock, and that all his arguments were so many waves breaking against it.

That afternoon he walked beside the sea with Mr Welland, who held a scarf to his throat and talked for an hour about draughts, doctors and the particular dangers of damp sheets. Archer listened with the patience of a future son-in-law, and discovered that the old man's anxious little world was as tightly closed as a jewel box. It occurred to him that he would spend a great many such afternoons in the years ahead, and the thought was not quite as pleasant as it should have been.

Toward evening, as they sat together under a tree with the sun going down, May turned to him with an expression of great seriousness and said that she wished to tell him something. If there were any other woman in his life, she said, she would never wish to hold him to his promise, for she believed that no happiness could be built on another person's sorrow. She spoke with a brave steadiness that cost her, he saw, a great deal of effort.

Archer took her hand and told her, with all the force of a man defending his honour, that there was no one else and that there never would be. He believed himself sincere, and in the narrowest sense he was, yet the words stuck in his throat like a coin too large to swallow. May smiled and said that she was glad, and the look of relief upon her face made him feel like a traitor.

A few days later Archer boarded the northbound train, having failed to win his early wedding and having promised to be patient. As the palms slid past the window and the air grew cooler mile by mile, he told himself that it was a small defeat and that the end would be the same. But the thought of Ellen Olenska, in her small house with its foreign lamps, rode with him all the way to New York.

Back in New York, Archer threw himself into the work of the office, and into the dinners, the visits and the evenings at the club that filled a gentleman's winter. Yet whenever there was a pause in the talk, or a quiet half hour before dinner, the thought of Ellen slipped in as softly as a cat and sat down in his mind. He found that the more firmly he declined to think of her, the more completely she occupied his thoughts.

One afternoon, at old Mrs Mingott's house, Ellen mentioned in a careless tone that she was going to Boston for a few days to visit a friend. She said nothing of her reason, and Archer, who knew that he had no right to ask, felt a disappointment out of all proportion to the news. He went home, ate his dinner in silence, and found that the whole evening had lost its colour.

Archer remembered that Mr Letterblair had papers to send to a lawyer in Boston, a small business that could well have waited a fortnight, and he begged leave to carry them himself. The old man, who suspected nothing at all, agreed with a kind and fatherly nod. Archer packed his bag that night with the quiet cunning of a schoolboy, taking care not to meet his own eyes in the mirror.

In Boston Archer delivered his papers with hurried politeness and went at once to the house where Ellen was staying, a tall, quiet house with a conservatory full of palms and ferns. Ellen was not in the room when he arrived, and in her place he found a slight, grey-eyed Frenchman who rose to greet him with the perfect manners of another world. The man gave his name as Monsieur Rivière, and Archer knew it before it was finished.

Monsieur Rivière explained in careful English that he had crossed the ocean with a message from the Count, who wished his wife to return and was prepared to be generous. Ellen had received him with great kindness, he said, and had refused him with even greater firmness. Archer saw that the visitor was not in the least angry, and that his voice held something that was almost relief.

Then, with the sadness of a man making a confession he has long wished to make, Monsieur Rivière admitted that it was he who had helped the Countess to leave her husband's house. No honest man, he said, could have watched her suffer in that place without trying to rescue her, and he had never regretted what he did. The rumours that had followed her across the ocean, he added gently, were as false as they were cruel.

Before he took his leave, Monsieur Rivière told Archer that the Countess was the bravest and most honest woman he had ever known, and that she needed good friends far more than she knew. He said it with such sincerity that Archer felt the words as a kind of charge laid upon him. Then the Frenchman bowed, took his hat, and went out into the grey Boston street, leaving behind him a silence full of questions.

Ellen came in a few minutes later, surprised and, he thought, a little glad, and she heard of his meeting with the Frenchman with a smile. They left the house and walked together to the Common, where the trees stood bare in the thin sunshine, and they found a bench that looked across the water. It was the first time they had ever been alone together out of doors, and neither of them quite knew what to say.

On the bench Ellen said gently that she knew perfectly well why he had come to Boston, and that the business of the papers had not deceived her for a moment. Archer did not deny it, and there followed a long silence in which they both looked at the bare trees and listened to the faraway murmur of the city. It was the nearest either of them had come to saying aloud what was in their hearts.

Ellen said that she loved her cousin May with all her heart, and that whatever they might feel they must never do anything to hurt her. Archer agreed, because there was nothing else he could honourably say, and on the train home he made up his mind to marry as soon as possible and to put his dangerous feelings behind a wall of duty. He did not yet understand that a wall of that kind is only as strong as the person who has to keep looking at it.

At the end of the winter the Wellands came home from Florida, and Archer was at the station to meet them with a bunch of flowers. May stepped down from the train brown from the southern sun and prettier than ever, and she greeted him with a smile in which there was not the smallest shadow. He felt a rush of affection for her that seemed, at that moment, almost as good as love.

He called on Mrs Welland in her heavy, comfortable drawing room and asked her, with all the eloquence he could muster, to let him marry May that spring. She was shocked, and murmured that it could not possibly be done, since the wedding clothes had to come from Paris and the linen had to be marked and the guests must be given proper notice. Archer, listening to her list of objections, felt like a man trying to move a mountain with a teaspoon.

In the end Mrs Welland was touched by his ardour, and she remembered, with a little shiver, that old Mrs Mingott had been asking for the wedding to be hurried. She sighed, pressed a handkerchief to her lips, and declared that if the dressmakers were willing the marriage might take place in the spring. Archer thanked her with more feeling than the occasion seemed to need, and she thought him the most devoted of young men.

May was delighted, and she flung her arms round her mother's neck and then, to the quiet amusement of the whole room, round his. Archer smiled and held her, and he felt a profound relief that the thing was settled, together with a strange, dull weight in his chest that he could neither explain nor shake off. He told himself that it was only the solemnity of the moment, and that every bridegroom must feel the same.

In the following weeks the wedding presents began to arrive at the Wellands' house, until the drawing room looked like a jeweller's shop. There were silver dishes and candlesticks, yards of old lace, and little boxes of gold and enamel, and each was entered with care in a notebook in May's neat hand. Every gift was a small proof of the world's approval, and Archer wondered why approval should make him feel so tightly held.

Mrs Archer, with the tender solemnity of a woman handing on a family treasure, brought out an old jewel that had belonged to her own mother and decided to give it to her future daughter-in-law. She took it to be reset in the fashion of the day, and talked of little else for a week, while Janey declared that no bride had ever received such an heirloom. Archer, watching them both, felt the whole weight of his family's love and could not feel that it was quite his own.

They had rented a small, new house, and one bright afternoon Archer and May walked from room to room, planning where each piece of furniture should stand. He asked for a plain library of his own, with books to the ceiling and a deep chair by the fire, and May agreed to everything with a smile that expressed no opinion whatever. He wondered, not for the first time, whether she had any wishes of her own, or whether her chief wish was to have none.

His friends gave him a bachelor dinner at a club, with a great deal of champagne and a great many jokes about the joys and perils of married life. Lefferts was brilliant, the others were noisy, and Archer laughed in the right places and drank to his own health with an expression of perfect happiness. Yet all through the evening he felt as if he were watching the party through a pane of glass.

Among the presents there came a small parcel from Ellen, with a note of only a few lines wishing him and May every happiness. Archer read it twice, though there was nothing in it that could not have been read aloud at the wedding breakfast. He held the little parcel in his hand for a long time before he put it away with the others, marvelling that so light an object could weigh so much upon the heart.

On the night before the wedding Archer lay awake in his room while the hours of the old house ticked slowly by. He told himself that he was doing the right and honourable thing, that May was good and loving and deserved a faithful husband, and that a dream he had no right to dream should be allowed to die. Toward dawn he fell asleep at last, with the strange sensation of a man who has agreed to a bargain whose terms he cannot quite remember.

On the wedding day Grace Church was crowded with the best families in New York, in their finest clothes, arranged by rank and by cousinship as precisely as the pieces on a chessboard. Old Mrs Mingott arrived in a carriage as vast as herself, and was helped up the aisle by two footmen amid a murmur of awe. Archer, waiting at the altar, found that he was gazing at the flowers with the careful attention of a man who does not wish to think.

When the organ began, May came slowly up the aisle on her father's arm, wrapped in a long white veil and carrying a spray of lilies of the valley. She looked radiant and serene, like a girl in an old painting, and a sigh of admiration went through the congregation. Archer's heart rose as it had done on the night of the opera, and for a moment he believed that everything would be well.

Before the minister they exchanged their vows, promising to love and cherish each other until death should part them. Archer pronounced the words in a clear, firm voice, as a man might sign a document that he fully intends to honour, while May spoke hers softly, with her eyes fixed upon his face. In the hush of the great church the ancient promises had a weight that he had never noticed before.

The bells rang out over the street as the newly married couple walked from the church into the bright spring sunshine, and the waiting crowd pressed forward to catch a glimpse of the bride. Friends threw flowers and called their good wishes, and a few of the younger bridesmaids wept openly with happiness. Archer helped May into the carriage and sat beside her, conscious of the rustle of her silk and the small, trembling hand in his.

At the wedding breakfast in the Wellands' house the guests drank the health of the bride and bridegroom in a fine old wine that had been kept for the purpose. Mr Welland made a short speech that moved everyone to tears, and he was so deeply affected that he forgot, for a whole quarter of an hour, to worry about the cold wind. Archer smiled at the right moments and accepted every kind word, and felt that he was playing a part in a play that had been written for him long ago.

That afternoon the young couple left for a quiet week in the country, before the long journey across the ocean that had been planned for them. May was cheerful and tender and entirely at ease, and she chatted about the wedding as they drove, while Archer tried hard to feel what a bridegroom is expected to feel. He was surprised to find how easy it was to act a part when one was grateful to be given one.

They sailed for Europe on one of the great steamers, and May enjoyed the voyage with the simple appetite of a healthy girl, never ill and never idle. Archer stood beside her at the rail and watched the grey water slide past, thinking of all the books he had meant to read and the places he had meant to see with a different companion. He put the thought away at once, and was ashamed, as a man is ashamed who has been caught reading another person's letter.

In Europe May stood smiling before every famous church and monument and declared that it was lovely, and she was cheerful, kind and punctual in all things. Yet she never asked a question, and never seemed to wish for an answer, and Archer began to see that what he had taken for innocence was largely the habit of not wondering. He felt, with a quiet dismay, how few things there were that the two of them truly shared.

In the evenings he tried reading poetry aloud to her on the balcony of their hotel, in the hope that she might learn to love the things that he loved. May listened with a sweet, attentive face, and when he had finished she asked whether he thought it would rain tomorrow, and whether she ought to take her umbrella. He laughed, and kissed her hand, and told himself that tenderness would be enough.

At the end of the long journey the Archers came home to New York, and a carriage set them down before their own front door in the evening light. The rooms were bright and orderly, with new flowers in every vase, and May moved through them with the quiet pride of a young mistress who has everything just as she wishes. Archer, following her, felt that a door had closed softly behind him, and that his life now lay before him in neat and familiar lines.

May filled the new house with flowers and arranged every room with a tact that seemed to come to her as naturally as breathing. Each cushion lay at its proper angle, each servant knew her duty, and every dinner began at exactly the hour on which it had been announced. Archer, passing from room to room, admired the order of it all, and could not help feeling that he had been placed in a very beautiful drawer.

Archer returned to the law office, where his days were filled with wills, trusts and the settlements of old families, a body of work that was respectable, dry and perfectly predictable. Mr Letterblair watched him with fatherly approval and spoke of a partnership in the future. The labour demanded only the surface of his mind, and the rest of it was free to wander where it had no business to go.

The Archers gave their first grand dinner, and to the delight of May's family the van der Luydens honoured it with their presence. The table glittered with the new silver, the courses followed one another with solemn precision, and when Louisa murmured at the end that the house was a model of good taste, May blushed with a pleasure that was almost religious. Archer drank his wine and felt that he had become a monument of his own good fortune.

When the guests had gone, Archer withdrew to the small library that he had insisted on having, and shut the door behind him. It was the only room in the house where nothing had been arranged to please anyone but himself, and the shelves of books rose around him like a quiet wall. He sat down in the deep chair, and for the first time in many hours he felt almost entirely like himself.

On Sundays the whole family dined at the Wellands', and the conversation never altered by a syllable. Mr Welland described his health and his doctors, Mrs Welland murmured sympathy, May's cousins exchanged news of weddings and funerals, and the old servant brought in the roast with a face of stone. Archer watched the faces round the table and wondered what would happen if one of them were suddenly to say something true.

At a reception in old Mrs Mingott's great house, Archer caught sight of Ellen on the far side of the room, listening with a patient smile to a lady in purple silk. When he crossed over, they exchanged only a few civil words, in the tone of two people who had agreed never to mention anything that mattered. He saw that she looked tired but calm, and he went away feeling that he had lost something that he had never owned.

That evening at home, May remarked that she thought the family had been rather unfair to poor Ellen, who must be lonely, and that she would like to ask her to dinner more often. She said it with such unaffected goodness that Archer was unable to answer for a moment. He thanked her, and found that her generosity, which should have pleased him, lay on his conscience like a stone.

As the warm weather came on, May and her family arranged to spend the summer at Newport, where the Wellands had a house by the sea, and where it was understood that all the best people went. Archer, who must remain at his desk through the heat, promised to join her at the end of every week. It was a plan that met with everyone's approval, and he agreed to it with a light heart that he felt to be slightly suspicious.

In June the city emptied, and the great houses stood shuttered under their dust sheets in the shimmering heat. Archer worked through the long evenings and ate his dinner alone at the club, among a few other abandoned husbands who spoke of nothing but the weather and the price of cotton. It was, he found, a curious relief to be alone, and he distrusted the relief.

At the end of the week Archer boarded the train for Newport, and as it ran through the green summer fields the heat of the city fell away from him like a garment. He opened the window and breathed the cool, salt air with a sense of release, and thought of May waiting for him on the lawn in her white dress. It was a pleasant thought, though he noticed that it did not quicken his pulse as another, forbidden thought could do.

At Newport Archer found May on the veranda of her family's house, which looked out over a lawn that sloped down to the sea. She wore a pale summer dress and a ribbon in her hair, and the whole place smelled of salt, roses and fresh-cut grass. It was impossible not to feel the beauty of the scene, and he felt, for a moment, that it was all that a man could wish for.

Newport in the summer was simply New York transported to the seaside, with the same families giving the same dinners and observing the same rules, only now with a view of the water. The ladies drove out each afternoon in open carriages, the gentlemen played at croquet or sailed their small boats, and nobody did anything that could be called an event. Archer found that he could predict, a week in advance, every sentence that would be spoken at every table.

That week a great garden party was held at one of the Newport cottages, and the chief attraction was to be an archery contest on the lawn. Archery was the fashionable sport of that summer, and every young lady who hoped to be admired came dressed in white with a quiver of arrows at her side. Targets were set up on the grass, and the whole company settled in chairs under striped awnings to watch.

One by one the young ladies stepped forward and drew their bows, and most of the arrows flew wide of the mark or fell short upon the grass. The audience applauded each attempt with the gentle courtesy of people who do not intend to be disappointed, and some of the gentlemen smothered their laughter behind their programmes. Only one or two of the girls showed real skill, and the best of them was yet to come.

Then May stepped forward in her white dress, and the whole lawn grew quiet. She drew her bow with a calm that was almost severe, as though she were performing some small duty to her family, and the arrow sped across the grass and struck the very heart of the target. A murmur of admiration rose from the spectators, and Archer, who had never seen her do anything difficult, felt his chest swell with surprise.

May won the prize, and the lawn rang with applause as she accepted it with a modest little curtsey that made everyone love her the more. Mrs Welland beamed upon the company like the mother of a queen, and a dozen ladies came forward to say that they had always known the girl had talent. Archer stood among the men who offered him their congratulations, and found, to his surprise, that he was able to be very proud.

At that moment Archer saw a woman in a pale dress appear at the far end of the lawn, walking slowly toward the awnings with her parasol over her shoulder. It was Ellen, arriving very late and quite alone, and she moved across the bright grass as though she had all the time in the world. He felt his heart give a heavy, unexpected beat, and he looked quickly at the target as if something there required his attention.

Ellen congratulated her cousin warmly, with a kiss on the cheek and a few words of praise that seemed to come from the heart. Then she turned to Archer and told him that marriage evidently agreed with him, and he found that he could not think of anything to say in reply. Her eyes rested on him for a moment with a look that was friendly and calm, and that was somehow more disturbing than coldness would have been.

Later in the afternoon he saw Ellen sitting alone on a veranda that overlooked the water, with her back to him and her face toward the sea. A small white sailboat was gliding toward the lighthouse on the point, and Archer made a secret bargain with himself that if she turned her head before the boat had passed the light, he would go to her. It was a foolish game, and he knew it, but he played it with the whole of his heart.

The little boat reached the lighthouse and slid slowly past it, and still Ellen did not turn her head, but sat motionless with her eyes upon the water. Archer stood where he was a moment longer, as though the rules of the game might still be bent, and then he turned and walked back toward the tents. He was hurt, and ashamed of being hurt, and he understood that something in him had quietly decided its direction.

With the first chill of autumn the Archers returned to New York, where the great houses opened their shutters and the winter season began to stir. Invitations arrived by the dozen, the opera was announced, and the calendars of the old families were filled with the same dinners that had been given the winter before. Archer took his place in the machine again with the dull sense of a man who has gone round once more upon a wheel.

At the opera Archer saw that Ellen was in the company of Julius Beaufort once more, and that the banker was leaning over her chair with the easy smile of a man who has never been refused. They talked in low voices while the great singers sang, and neither of them seemed to be paying the slightest attention to the music. Archer, watching from across the house, felt something in his chest tighten like a screw.

At home he found that he could not forget what he had seen, and he walked up and down his little library with a jealousy that astonished him by its violence. It was bitter to realise that a married man had no right to such a feeling, and that his wife's cousin owed him nothing whatever, not even an explanation. He told himself severely that he was behaving like a fool, and he went on behaving like one.

One day Mr Letterblair remarked to Archer, in a low and careful voice, that he would not leave a penny of his own in Beaufort's bank. In forty years of practice, he said, he had seen a great many handsome houses built on very weak foundations, and he disliked the way that this one was so loudly admired. Archer, who had thought of Beaufort chiefly as a rival, was startled to discover that he might also be a danger.

At the club the older men began to murmur that Julius Beaufort's affairs were not as sound as they appeared, and that some of his speculations had been unwise. Yet Beaufort still drove the finest horses in New York and gave the most splendid entertainments, and nobody dared to say aloud what everybody was thinking. It was the way of that world to look away from a danger until it had become a catastrophe.

One grey morning a rumour ran through the streets that Beaufort's bank could not pay its debts, and a crowd of anxious depositors gathered at its doors. The clerks looked pale, the shutters were half drawn, and the old gentlemen who had trusted him with their savings stood about like mourners at a funeral. Within an hour the whole of New York knew, and by evening nobody could remember ever having liked the man.

By evening the bank had closed its doors for good, and Julius Beaufort stood alone in his empty office while the last of the clerks filed out with their coats upon their arms. The man who had owned the best horses and the finest ballroom in New York was ruined, and his proud face had turned the colour of ash. In the silence of that room, the money that had made him great seemed to have been nothing but a story that everyone had agreed to believe.

The great Beaufort house stood dark and silent, its ballroom covered once more in dust sheets, and not a single carriage stopped at its door. The same people who had eaten at Beaufort's table and drunk his wine now said that they had always suspected he was not quite one of them. It was a lesson in the swiftness with which a society that is generous to success can become merciless to failure.

Regina Beaufort, pale but upright in her plain black dress, went from house to house among her relatives and asked them to stand by her in her trouble. They were polite and tender and full of sympathy, but each of them made it clear, in a different way, that nobody could be expected to help a man who had been careless with other people's money. Archer saw that the loyalty of the old families stopped exactly where their own honour began.

May said that she was very sorry for poor Regina, but that a woman must not ask her family to forgive a wrong, and that the family were quite right to be firm. She spoke with the clear certainty of a person who has never had to doubt which side honour was on. Archer, listening, felt that her sense of right was complete and perfect, and he could not decide whether it was the most admirable thing about her or the most terrible.

Not long afterward the news ran through the family that old Mrs Mingott had suffered a stroke, and the relatives hurried to her great house in a flutter of black silk and anxiety. The doctors spoke gravely, and for some days nobody knew whether the formidable old lady would live. Yet, lying in her huge bed with one side of her face a little strange, she was found to be as clear in her mind as ever, and she asked at once for Ellen.

Ellen left her little house and came to live in the great house, where she nursed her grandmother day and night with a patience that astonished the family. The old lady would have nobody else near her, and her relations, who had never forgiven Ellen her adventures, were obliged to see her in a gentler light. It was remarkable how quickly a scandal could be forgotten when the scandalous person was found to be useful.

Archer went to the great house to ask after the old lady, and it was Ellen who came down the stairs to speak to him, pale from lack of sleep and with her sleeves pushed back. They had not been alone together for many months, and the hall, with its heavy clock and its closed doors, seemed to hold its breath. He asked about her grandmother in a voice that did not sound like his own.

Ellen said that she was deeply sorry for Regina Beaufort, and that she had seen Julius Beaufort so often only because he could talk of the great world beyond New York. She spoke without a trace of embarrassment, and the whole mean fabric of Archer's jealousy dissolved in a moment. He was ashamed to have built such a thing, and yet more glad than he could say to have lost it.

As he was leaving, Ellen mentioned, in a tone of perfect carelessness, that she sometimes escaped to the Metropolitan Museum on her free afternoons, since it was the only quiet place in town. She did not ask him to come, and she did not look at him as she spoke. But he understood her perfectly, and he walked home through the grey streets with the beating of a schoolboy's heart.

On the afternoon he had chosen, Archer walked into the Metropolitan Museum and found its long rooms almost empty, with only a sleepy attendant dozing beside a case of ancient relics. His footsteps echoed among the old clay vessels and little carved figures that had been dug from the earth of a distant island. He had never in his life been so conscious of silence, nor so afraid of what it might be waiting to hear.

He found Ellen standing before a glass case of old cups and carved figures, in a dark dress and a small hat, with her back to the door. She turned and smiled, and remarked that nothing in New York was so restful as a room full of things that had been forgotten for so many centuries. There was a lightness in her tone, but he saw that her hands were pressed together as though to keep them steady.

At last Archer could hold back no longer, and in a low voice that shook a little he told her that he loved her and had loved her almost from the first night. He said that he had made a terrible mistake in marrying, that he could not go on pretending, and that he was sick of the world of masks in which they both lived. She listened with her face turned away, and for a long moment did not speak.

Ellen answered at last that she could not build her happiness on May's pain, and that she had come back from Europe precisely to escape the sort of life he was now describing. When he begged her to go away with him, she asked him, with a sad and gentle smile, where in the whole world they could possibly go. There was no such country, she said, and he knew in his heart that she was right.

They left the museum without having decided anything, and stood for a moment on the steps in the cold grey light, neither of them able to say goodbye. The park trees were bare, a few carriages rolled along the drive, and the world went on exactly as before. It seemed to Archer extraordinary that his whole life should have been changed by a conversation among old clay cups, and that nobody passing could see it.

After that afternoon Archer found that he could not work, and he sat at his desk for an hour at a time with the same page of the same document before him. At home May noticed that he was pale, and suggested with tender anxiety that he was overworking, and that he should take more exercise and eat a little more at dinner. He thanked her, and felt that her kindness was a form of imprisonment more complete than any lock.

A short note arrived from Ellen, who had gone to Washington for a few days while her grandmother was recovering. She wrote that she would return on Thursday evening and asked, in four simple lines, whether he would meet her at the ferry, since she had something to say to him that could not be put on paper. He read it standing in the hall, and put it carefully into an inside pocket, where it seemed to burn.

On Thursday evening he crossed the Hudson on the ferry, with the dark water slapping against the bows and the lamps of the city dwindling behind him in a yellow haze. He stood alone on the deck in the cold, rehearsing sentences that he knew he would never say, and listening to the beating of his own heart. In the station on the far shore the great clock showed that the train was five minutes late.

Ellen stepped from the train in a dark travelling cloak, tired from the long journey and holding a small bag in one gloved hand. When she saw him her whole face lit up, and for a moment neither of them could speak, so complete was the happiness of simply being in the same place. Then she took his arm, and they walked together through the crowd to the carriage that was waiting outside.

In the dark, closed carriage they sat close together while the wheels rattled over the stones, and after a long silence Archer took her gloved hand in both of his. She did not take it away, and he felt through the thin leather the warmth and the trembling of her fingers. It was the first time in all those months that either of them had admitted, by a single gesture, that there was something to be admitted.

Ellen said, in a low and steady voice, that she knew exactly what it meant to be a secret love, because she had seen such lives in Europe, in hotels and hidden rooms. She would not be that sort of woman, and she would not make him that sort of man, a creature of cheap excuses who was afraid of being found. Archer, who had prepared a hundred arguments, found that they all fell away before the plain dignity of her refusal.

Ellen told him that she could love him only by giving him up, since if she took what he offered they would both become smaller, and the love that had made them better would turn into something ordinary and sad. It was because she loved him, she said, that she wanted him to remain the man who was worth loving. He understood the argument with perfect clarity, and hated it with all his heart.

Archer protested fiercely that they were throwing away their lives to please a crowd of people who did not care for them, and that May's peace was built upon a lie that the truth would be kinder to end. Ellen answered that she had come back to escape from lies, and that she would not begin her new life by robbing someone who had been so good to her. There was no answer to that, and he sat back against the cushions in silence.

At last the carriage drew up before old Mrs Mingott's great house, where a single lamp was burning in the hall. Ellen pressed his hand once, very hard, and stepped down into the cold without looking back at him. The door opened and closed upon her, and Archer remained in the dark carriage, listening to the horses stamping on the frozen street.

Archer sent the carriage away and walked home alone through the cold streets, with his collar turned up and his thoughts going round like a mill-wheel. He understood her reasons perfectly, and he even admired them, but he could not persuade himself that a story of this kind must end with a handshake on a doorstep. The lamps of the empty avenue burned steadily ahead of him, like a row of patient questions.

A few days later, in the quiet hall of old Mrs Mingott's house, Ellen told him that she had decided to go back to Europe. Her grandmother, who understood a great deal more than she ever said, had promised her enough money to live independently, and Ellen meant to settle in Paris. She spoke quite gently, with the air of a woman who has settled the matter with herself and wishes to be spared any further effort.

Archer told her, in a low voice that did not allow of argument, that he would follow her across the ocean, and that no convention could hold him back. Ellen said only that he must not, that he must remember May, and that this was the last time he should speak to her of such things. But she did not withdraw her hands from his, and her eyes admitted that the answer she had given was not the one her heart desired.

That night Archer sat in his library and planned what he would say to May, choosing every word with the care of a man drafting a legal document. He would tell her the truth, honestly and without excuse, and he would ask her to forgive him and to set him free. It was the most terrible thing he had ever resolved to do, and he was surprised to feel, beneath the fear, a strange and steady joy.

The next evening he came home early, resolved to speak before his courage could cool. He found May sitting quietly beside the lamp with her sewing in her lap, and when she looked up at him there was a shy, strange light in her face that he had never seen there before. The speech that he had prepared with such care went out of his head at the sight of it.

Before he could say a word, May told him softly that she had something to say, and that she had waited until she was quite certain. The doctor had been that day, she said, and in a few months they were going to have a child. She said it with a blush and a smile, and with a light in her eyes of such complete and trusting happiness that Archer's whole speech turned to ashes in his mouth.

Archer knelt beside her chair and held her hands, unable for a moment to speak, and she bent to kiss his forehead. She told him, as though it were a small and happy detail, that she had spoken of it to Ellen two weeks ago, on the afternoon of their talk, though at the time she had not been certain. Archer felt the whole room tilt gently as the meaning of the date reached him.

In the stillness of the room he understood that Ellen had known of the child on the night in the carriage, when she had refused him and told him that she could love him only by giving him up. She had said nothing of it, because the secret was not hers to tell, and she had borne it in silence while he pleaded. He thought of her calm face in the dark, and his admiration was so deep that it was almost a kind of pain.

Late that night Archer sat alone in his library and knew that he could not abandon a wife who was about to become a mother, nor set a child's name against a scandal. The door that he had meant to force had been closed by a gentle hand, and what he felt was less despair than a kind of exhausted calm. He told himself that this, after all, was what honour meant, and wondered why honour should be so cold.

Within a day both families had heard the news, and the grandmothers wept with joy in each other's arms, while Mr Welland sat down heavily and said that he felt twenty years younger. Mrs Archer inquired whether the old family cradle might be fetched from the attic, and Janey began to knit tiny garments in colours that nobody could have chosen. Archer received the congratulations of everyone he met, and felt the walls of his life moving gently closer.

A few days later May told him that dear Ellen was going back to Europe, as if he might not have heard it, and that she wished to give a farewell dinner in her honour. The whole family must come, she said, so that Ellen might see how much they all loved her and how sorry they were to let her go. Archer listened with a face of stone, and agreed, because he could think of no reason in the world that he could give for refusing.

May wrote the invitations in her neat, upright hand, and the replies came back by return of post, every one of them an acceptance. Archer remembered the cold little notes of refusal that had greeted the Mingotts' dinner in Ellen's first winter, and the change was so complete that it seemed almost a joke. It was only in the act of leaving that New York found it could be generous to Ellen.

On the night of the dinner the whole clan gathered in the Archers' drawing room, the van der Luydens in their stately black, the Mingotts and the Wellands in their best silks, and Archer's mother in her old lace. The candles gleamed on the silver, the flowers stood in perfect order, and the room had the hushed solemnity of an occasion at which nothing could possibly go wrong. It was, he thought, like a funeral to which everybody had agreed to bring their finest clothes.

Ellen arrived last, in a pale gown with a thin ribbon at her throat, and she stood in the doorway for a moment, perfectly calm, while the room turned toward her. May kissed her warmly and led her to the place of honour at the table, with a sweetness so complete that it was impossible to detect any seam. Archer, standing by his chair, felt the blood go out of his face and made an effort to look like a host.

Throughout the dinner the whole family was kind to Ellen, and they spoke with admirable warmth of her return to Europe, which was where, they agreed, such a person naturally belonged. Mrs Welland said that Paris would suit her exactly, Mr Welland hoped that she would take every precaution against the sea air, and the van der Luydens drank her health with a gravity that was almost ceremonial. Each speech was a little more affectionate than the last, and Archer began to hear in the affection the sound of a door being closed.

Archer looked down the long table at the smiling faces of his family and saw that each of them wore precisely the same expression, an expression of kindly and watchful relief. They talked and laughed and passed the dishes, but their eyes returned again and again to the two of them, to himself and to Ellen, as the eyes of a guard return to a prisoner. A cold suspicion began to stir in him, and it grew with every course.

At last he understood, with a clearness that was almost physical, that the whole family had guessed his feeling for Ellen and had worked together in perfect silence to keep them apart. The dinner was not a farewell but a ritual of closing ranks, performed by a tribe that had seen one of its members in danger and had quietly surrounded him. Nobody had said a word, and nobody ever would, and that, he saw, was the whole genius of the thing.

From the other end of the table May smiled at him with perfect sweetness, and he wondered, for the first time in his life, how much she knew and how much of this evening had been her design. Her kindness to Ellen, her tender announcement, even the date of the confidence that she had made, now seemed to him part of a pattern too delicate to be an accident. He could find no trace of malice in her face, only a calm and serene determination to keep her happiness.

In the hall, while the maids brought the cloaks, Ellen said goodbye to Archer in the polite phrases that she used to everyone, and held out her gloved hand as lightly as a flower. Yet her fingers stayed in his a moment longer than courtesy required, and her eyes rested on his face with an expression that held everything they had never said. Then she turned to May and kissed her warmly, and the moment, like so many others, was gone for ever.

She stepped into her carriage at the door, and the horses moved off into the winter night, their harness chiming faintly in the cold. Archer stood on the step and watched the two small lamps dwindle down the street until they were swallowed by the dark, and he did not call out, and he did not follow. It was the most difficult act of his life, and it consisted entirely of doing nothing.

He went back into the house, where May was waiting for him in the lamplit hall with a gentle smile, and she said that dear Ellen had looked quite lovely tonight. Archer agreed with her gravely, because there was nothing else that he could say, and she slipped her hand through his arm as they went in to say goodnight to the last of the guests. It was the first of a great many evenings on which he would take that arm, and he took it as a man takes up a duty.

In the spring May gave birth to a healthy son, who was christened Dallas, and Archer held the tiny creature in his arms with a wonder that he had not expected. May lay smiling against the pillows, pale and triumphant, and the old house filled with the quiet rustle of aunts and nurses. He felt for the first time that his life had a direction that was entirely independent of his own desires.

As Dallas grew, he became the delight of his father's life, and on Sundays they walked in the park while he asked questions that no one of the older generation would have dared to put. Archer answered as honestly as he could, and felt that in doing so he was repairing something that had been broken long before the child was born. It was a happiness of a different kind from the one he had once dreamed of, but it was real.

Two more children followed, a daughter and then another son, and the quiet house grew noisy with nurses, toys and the sound of small feet on the stairs. May was a devoted and tireless mother, who taught her children to be honest, kind and perfectly well behaved, and who never in all those years raised her voice. Archer watched her with admiration and with a certain remoteness, as a man watches a distant, well-lit house from a train.

The years passed, and Archer became a respected citizen of the kind that New York had begun to need, one who sat upon committees, signed petitions and worked patiently for honest government. His hair turned grey at the temples, and his name was spoken in the clubs with the mild respect that is given to a man who has never done anything surprising. Yet he did his duty with sincerity, and he believed that it was not a small thing to have done.

New York changed with bewildering speed in those years, as new money, new buildings and new manners flooded into a city that had once been ruled by a handful of families. The old houses of the avenue were pulled down one by one to make room for shops and hotels, and the rules that had seemed as permanent as the stars were quietly forgotten. Archer watched it all with a mixture of regret and amusement, for he had always suspected that the rules were more fragile than they looked.

One by one the old people of that world departed, and among them, at last, was the great Mrs Mingott, who met death as she had met everything else in life, with courage and a certain scornful good humour. Archer stood among the black-clad relations at the funeral and felt that a whole age was closing, and that he himself, though not yet old, was being quietly moved to the front. The people who had made the rules were nearly all gone, and the rules had survived them only as habits.

In all those years Archer never wrote to Ellen, never went to Europe to seek her, and never spoke of her to a living soul. But he kept the memory of her in a private chamber of his mind, a small, quiet room to which he alone had the key, and where nothing was ever allowed to change. He visited it rarely, and always with the reverence of a man entering a church, and he came away each time a little steadier.

Dallas grew into a tall, cheerful young man who said exactly what he thought and seemed to have no idea that anyone had ever done otherwise. Archer listened to him with amazement and delight, for the frankness that came so easily to the boy was a thing that his own generation had never learned and had scarcely dared to imagine. It sometimes seemed to him that the whole world had been quietly opened while he was looking elsewhere.

One winter one of the children fell seriously ill, and May nursed the child through the long nights with the same quiet, unselfish devotion that she gave to everything. The child recovered, but May herself caught the fever and sank rapidly, and the doctors, for all their skill, could do nothing to stop the illness. Archer sat beside her bed through the final days, holding her hand with a feeling that he had no name for.

May died, and Archer stood beside her grave on a grey winter day with his three children round him, mourning her with a sincerity that surprised him. She had been a good wife, a devoted mother and a woman of perfect honour, and he knew that he would never find another like her. If there had been a part of his heart that she had never reached, it was no fault of hers, and he stood bareheaded in the cold and honoured her for what she had been.

More years went by, and Archer lived on alone in the quiet house, a grey-haired widower whose children had grown and gone out into their own lives. He filled the evenings with books and the long habit of duty, and found, with some surprise, that he was not unhappy. He had learned, in those quiet evenings, that a man may be perfectly content without ever being fulfilled, and that the world does not mind the difference.

One evening Dallas announced, with the cheerful directness that was his nature, that he was going to marry Fanny Beaufort, the daughter of the once-disgraced banker. Archer could not help smiling at the irony, for the scandal that had shaken the whole of old New York had faded so completely that nobody now thought it worth mentioning. He said that he was delighted, and was a little surprised to discover that he meant every word of it.

Dallas said that nobody cared any longer about the old rules, and that the only thing that mattered about a girl was whether he loved her and she loved him. Archer listened, and thought how his own generation would have found such a sentence unthinkable, and how many lives might have been different if it had been thinkable. He kept those thoughts to himself, and merely pressed his son's shoulder with a warmth that said all he could not.

Dallas suggested that before the wedding the two of them should take a last holiday together in Europe, as a kind of farewell to their life as two men in one house. Archer had not crossed the ocean for many years, and he hesitated, remembering how deliberately he had stayed at home, but in the end he laughed and said yes. They sailed in the spring, and he stood on the deck beside his son with the feeling that something long delayed was drawing near.

In Paris Archer and Dallas walked beside the river in the soft afternoon light, among bookstalls, bridges and the grey, gold-tinted stone of the old city. Archer had not seen Paris for many years, and he found it more beautiful than he remembered and a little more painful than he had expected. He looked at every street corner as though it might hold a shadow that he knew.

Over coffee at a table outside a cafe, Dallas remarked in an easy voice that he had arranged to visit Countess Olenska the next afternoon, since he could hardly pass through Paris without calling. Archer's spoon stopped halfway to his cup, and for a moment the boulevard seemed to go silent. He asked, with a calm that astonished him, how his son knew where she lived.

Dallas looked at his father with great gentleness and said that before she died his mother had told him something that he thought Archer ought to know. She had said that she was quite safe in leaving the children with him, because once, when she had asked him, he had given up the thing that he wanted most in the world. Archer sat quite motionless, and heard the noise of the boulevard go by as if it were happening in a different country.

Archer rose from the table and walked a little way along the street, and stopped with his hat in his hand, like a man in church. He understood at last that May had known everything, from the very beginning, and that she had never said a word and never once let him feel that she knew. It was the most complete generosity he had ever met, and it had been given to him for more than twenty years without his noticing.

Dallas asked, very kindly, whether it had been Ellen whom his father had given up, and Archer, after a long moment, answered that it had, and that she had been the only woman he had ever truly wanted. He said that in his time people had not thought it right to throw away everything they had for the sake of one love, and that perhaps they were not all wrong. Dallas smiled, and did not argue, and took his father's arm as they walked on.

That night, in the hotel, Archer could not sleep, and he stood for a long time at the window watching the lamps of Paris glimmer along the avenue below. He wondered whether Ellen had changed, whether she would know him with his grey hair and his heavy step, and whether she had ever, in all those years, thought of a closed carriage on a winter night. By morning he had decided nothing, and knew only that the day would not be like any other.

The next afternoon, under a warm and cloudless sky, Archer and Dallas walked through the bright streets toward the Invalides, where the great golden dome shone like a second sun above the roofs. Dallas talked cheerfully of buildings, of Fanny and of the future, and Archer answered him at random, hearing the voice as one hears a stream through a wall. Every step brought him nearer to a door that he had closed in his own mind more than twenty years before.

They came at last to a wide, quiet square, shaded by chestnut trees, with benches along the edge of the pavement and tall pale houses standing in the afternoon sun. A few children played beside a fountain, and an old man was reading his newspaper in the shade, as though nothing in the world were happening. Dallas said that the Countess lived somewhere here, and Archer found that his legs had suddenly become heavy.

Dallas stopped and pointed up at a high balcony on the fifth floor of one of the tall buildings, where a striped sunshade had been drawn out against the glare. That was the place, he said cheerfully, and Archer stood still in the middle of the square, with his hat in his hand, unable to move another step. The balcony looked very far away, and the space between it and him seemed to be made of all the years he had lived.

Dallas turned in surprise and asked his father why he had stopped, and whether he was feeling ill. Archer answered that he was perfectly well and that he did not think he would go up after all, and he heard his own voice say it with a calm that seemed to belong to somebody else. Dallas stared at him, and then, with the quickness that was one of his best qualities, he seemed to understand.

Archer lowered himself onto a bench at the edge of the square and told his son to go up without him. Dallas might say to the Countess, he said, that his father was old-fashioned, and that this would be explanation enough, and then he waved him gently away. Dallas hesitated for a long moment, with his hand on his father's shoulder, and then he went.

Dallas crossed the square and passed through the door of the tall building, which closed behind him with a soft sound that Archer felt rather than heard. The grey-haired man settled himself on the bench and fixed his eyes upon the far balcony with its striped sunshade, as though it were a window into another century. He knew almost exactly how long it would take his son to climb the stairs, and he counted the moments one by one.

On the bench Archer imagined the room beyond the balcony, a room full of soft lamps and rugs and strange flowers, not unlike the little room that he had once visited on a winter afternoon. He pictured Ellen rising from her chair at the sound of the bell, and seeing a tall young man in the doorway who had his father's eyes and his mother's smile. It was so clear to him that he could almost hear the tone in which she would say his name.

Archer sat quite still, with the sun on his face and his eyes upon the high window, and he felt a strange peace settle over him. Ellen seemed more real to him here on the bench, in the clear light of memory, than she could be upstairs, where he would find a woman who had lived without him for many years. He had loved her for so long and so quietly that the love had become a country of his own, and he did not wish to leave it for a visit.

At last a servant came out on the balcony, drew in the striped sunshade, and closed the tall shutters one by one against the afternoon light. Archer watched the gesture with a feeling that was neither grief nor surprise, but something quieter, like the sound of a book being closed. He understood that his son's visit was over, that the room above had been put away for the evening, and that nothing remained for him to do.

Archer got up slowly from the bench and walked back alone toward his hotel through the soft Paris dusk, past lighted cafes and the long avenues where the first lamps were beginning to glow. He did not look back at the balcony, for he had no need to, since everything that had mattered to him lay behind him already in the ordered silence of his memory. Dallas would give his account that evening, and Archer would listen gravely, and the age of innocence would remain, as it always had, a thing that could not be returned to.
